overview.about: An MBA is not only frameworks — it is a way of thinking shaped by a handful of great minds and hundreds of cases. Here you meet Drucker, Porter, Christensen, Deming, Buffett and Munger, Grove, Collins, Kahneman, Prahalad, Mintzberg and Senge, then work through case studies in the Harvard style: the situation, the decision, what happened and what you would do.

chapters.title: Peter Drucker: the man who invented management

cards.title: Why Drucker matters
cards.body: Peter Drucker (1909–2005), an Austrian-born writer who settled in the US, treated management as a **discipline** you could study and teach — not a talent you were born with. His 1946 study of General Motors and *The Practice of Management* (1954) shaped how companies like GE, P&G and later Indian groups organised themselves.

cards.title: The purpose of a business
cards.body: Drucker's most famous line: the purpose of a business is to **create a customer**. Profit is not the purpose; it is the test of whether you are doing the job well and the cost of staying in business. So every firm has two core functions: **marketing** and **innovation**. Everything else is a cost.

cards.title: "What is our business?"
cards.body: Drucker said this question is hardest to answer when the business is succeeding. The answer comes from the **customer's** side: who is the customer, where are they, what do they buy, and what do they value? A railway that thinks it is in 'railways' and not 'transport' gets blindsided.

cards.title: Management by objectives (MBO)
cards.body: Introduced in *The Practice of Management*. Manager and subordinate **jointly agree** a few measurable objectives that roll up to company goals, then the person is free to choose how to hit them. The key word is **self-control**: people steer by their own results, not by the boss's orders.

cards.title: The knowledge worker
cards.body: Drucker coined 'knowledge worker' (around 1959) for people who work with their minds — engineers, analysts, doctors, coders. They own the means of production (their brain), so they cannot be supervised like factory hands. The manager's job shifts to **making their productivity possible**: clear goals, autonomy, continuous learning.

cards.title: The Effective Executive
cards.body: Drucker's 1966 book says effectiveness is a **habit** that can be learnt: (1) know where your time goes, (2) focus on contribution, not effort, (3) build on strengths, not weaknesses, (4) do first things first — one at a time, (5) make few but fundamental decisions.

cards.title: Drucker in an Indian bank branch
cards.body: A branch manager sets MBO with a relationship officer: grow SME deposits 15%, keep NPAs under 2%, two product-cross-sells per client. The officer decides which clusters to visit. Every month they review results together. That is MBO; a branch that just counts 'calls made' is measuring activity, not contribution.

cards.q: According to Drucker, what is the purpose of a business?
cards.explain: Drucker argued the only valid purpose is to create a customer; profit is the test and the reward, not the purpose.

cards.q: The crucial idea that makes MBO work, in Drucker's original version, is:
options: Self-control by the employee against agreed objectives
cards.explain: Drucker called it 'management by objectives and self-control' — jointly set goals, then the person steers themselves.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of Drucker's practices of the effective executive?
cards.explain: Drucker explicitly said build on strengths — make weaknesses irrelevant rather than trying to fix all of them.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Before Drucker, 'management' mostly meant either Frederick Taylor's time-and-motion engineering or the instincts of a founder. Drucker argued that managing is a **discipline** — a set of practices that can be learned — and that managers exist to make people productive together. Born in Vienna in 1909, he worked as a journalist in Germany, fled the Nazis, and in the US was invited to study General Motors from the inside. That study, *Concept of the Corporation* (1946), was the first serious look at how a giant company actually runs.

His central claim is simple: **a business exists to create a customer.** Profit matters enormously, but as a test of performance and as the premium for risk — not as the reason the firm exists. That single shift of perspective, from inside-out to outside-in, drives everything else he wrote.

In *The Practice of Management* (1954) Drucker said the most important question a top team can ask is **'What is our business — and what should it be?'** The answer is never found by looking at your factories or products. It is found by looking at the customer: who are they, what do they buy, what do they consider 'value'?

He later framed this as the **theory of the business** (HBR, 1994): every organisation runs on assumptions about its environment, its mission and its core competencies. When reality changes and the assumptions don't, even a well-run company declines. His advice: ask the question most seriously when you are **successful**, because success makes the old answer feel permanent.

notes.h: Idea 2: Management by objectives and self-control
notes.p: MBO is Drucker's most-used tool. The steps:
points: 1. Company goals are set for a period.
2. Each manager, with their boss, agrees a **few** measurable objectives that contribute to those goals.
3. The manager chooses the means — this is the **self-control** part.
4. Results are reviewed regularly against the objectives, not against effort or activity.
5. Objectives are reset for the next period.

notes.h: Idea 3: The knowledge worker and the effective executive
notes.p:
Drucker coined 'knowledge worker' around 1959, predicting that the economy would come to depend on people who are paid to think. Infosys, TCS, every hospital and every consulting firm is a knowledge organisation. You can't supervise a coder's thinking hour by hour; you can only define the contribution you need and remove obstacles. Hence his line that knowledge workers must be managed **as if they were volunteers**.

*The Effective Executive* (1966) applies this to yourself. Five habits: record and prune where your **time** goes (most executives guess badly); ask 'what can **I contribute**?' rather than 'what am I busy with?'; staff and work from **strengths**; concentrate on **one thing at a time**; and make a few big, well-thought **decisions** rather than many small ones.

notes.h: Applying Drucker today: Indian and global cases
notes.p:
**Global:** GE under Jack Welch adopted Drucker's question 'If you weren't already in this business, would you enter it today?' — leading to the rule that GE would be number one or two in each business, or fix, sell or close it.

**India:** When Indian telecom shifted from voice to data, operators who defined their business as 'selling minutes' were caught out; the right Drucker answer was 'connecting customers to what they want — content, payments, commerce'. Similarly, a family-run FMCG distributor in Indore that asks 'who is our real customer — the kirana owner or the shopper?' may decide its job is to help kiranas sell faster (credit, ordering app, merchandising), not just to deliver cartons.

**Worked example of MBO done right vs wrong.** A sales head sets a team goal of ₹10 crore annual revenue. Bad MBO: divide it equally, ₹1 crore each for 10 reps, and track 'calls per day'. Good MBO: each rep and manager agree targets from territory potential (say ₹1.4 crore in Pune, ₹0.7 crore in a newer market), add one quality objective (repeat-purchase rate ≥ 60%), and the rep chooses how to get there. Same ₹10 crore total, but the targets are believable and owned.

Drucker's writing is full of wisdom but light on data, so academics criticise it as hard to test. MBO in practice often degenerates into **top-down targets** with bonuses attached — exactly what Drucker warned against — and W. Edwards Deming attacked numerical targets for encouraging gaming. A narrow, metrics-only MBO can also crowd out work that is hard to measure (mentoring, safety, innovation). Finally, 'create a customer' can be misread to justify chasing growth at any cost; Drucker himself insisted profit must cover the true cost of capital.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: In MBA interviews you'll be asked 'What business is X really in?' — answer from the customer side. In strategy and OB exams, MBO and the knowledge worker are standard short-answer topics; mention **self-control** and joint goal-setting. On the job, your first appraisal cycle *is* MBO (or its modern cousin OKRs): negotiate a few outcome-based goals, not a list of activities.

points: Drucker (1909–2005) made management a teachable **discipline**; studied GM in *Concept of the Corporation* (1946).
Purpose of a business = **create a customer**; profit is the test, not the purpose.
Two basic functions: **marketing and innovation**.
'What is our business?' — answer from the customer; revisit it when successful. Later called the **theory of the business**.
**MBO** (*The Practice of Management*, 1954): jointly agreed, measurable objectives + **self-control** over means.
Coined **knowledge worker**; manage them like volunteers.
*The Effective Executive*: time, contribution, strengths, first things first, few big decisions.
Critique: little data; MBO often turns into top-down targets that invite gaming.

chapters.title: Michael Porter: competitive advantage and shared value

cards.title: Strategy as economics
cards.body: Michael Porter, a Harvard professor trained in industrial economics, gave strategy its toolkit: **Five Forces** (1979 HBR article; *Competitive Strategy*, 1980), **generic strategies** and the **value chain** (*Competitive Advantage*, 1985). His core question: why do some industries and firms earn persistently higher profits than others?

cards.title: Five Forces
cards.body: An industry's profitability depends on five forces: **rivalry** among existing firms, **threat of new entrants**, **threat of substitutes**, **bargaining power of buyers** and **bargaining power of suppliers**. Strong forces squeeze profits (airlines); weak forces leave room for high returns (a patented drug, a dominant software platform).

cards.title: Three generic strategies
cards.body: To beat rivals you either be the **cost leader** (lowest cost, price at or near average, pocket the margin), **differentiate** (be unique on something buyers pay a premium for), or **focus** on a narrow segment with cost or differentiation. Trying to be everything risks being **'stuck in the middle'**.

cards.title: The value chain
cards.body: A firm is a chain of activities: **primary** (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, service) and **support** (infrastructure, HR, technology, procurement). Advantage comes from performing activities **cheaper or differently** — and from how they fit together.

cards.title: "What Is Strategy?" (1996)
cards.body: Porter's most-cited essay: **operational effectiveness is not strategy.** Doing the same things better (lean, benchmarking) is necessary but easy to copy. Strategy means choosing a **unique position**, making **trade-offs** (deciding what NOT to do) and creating **fit** among activities so the whole system is hard to imitate.

cards.title: Fit in action: IndiGo
cards.body: IndiGo built its position around low cost and on-time performance: a largely single-family Airbus fleet, quick turnarounds, no-frills service, high aircraft use. Each choice reinforces the others — a rival copying one piece (say, cheap fares) without the rest can't match its costs. That is Porter's **fit**.

cards.title: Creating shared value (2011)
cards.body: With Mark Kramer, Porter argued firms can find profit by solving **social problems**: redesign products for unmet needs, raise productivity in the value chain (e.g. water, energy, supplier health), and build local clusters. Unlike CSR, shared value is meant to be **core strategy**, not philanthropy.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT one of Porter's Five Forces?
cards.explain: Regulation affects the forces (e.g. raising entry barriers) but Porter does not list it as a sixth force.

cards.q: Per Porter's 1996 essay, which is the strongest source of sustainable advantage?
options: A unique position with trade-offs and fit among activities
cards.explain: Operational effectiveness is easily copied; a system of activities that fit together with clear trade-offs is hard to imitate.

cards.q: A firm that tries to be both cheapest and most premium across all segments risks being:
cards.explain: Porter warned that firms without a clear generic strategy end up 'stuck in the middle' with no advantage.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Michael Porter asks two questions. First: **is this industry attractive?** Some industries (soft drinks concentrate, enterprise software) earn high returns for decades; others (airlines, basic steel) struggle. Second: **within the industry, how is this firm positioned?** A great firm in a bad industry can still win, and a sloppy firm in a great industry can still lose.

Porter, trained in economics at Harvard, borrowed from industrial-organisation theory and turned it into tools a manager can use: Five Forces, generic strategies, the value chain, and later the idea of shared value.
Profit in an industry is a pie. The five forces decide how much of the pie the firms get to keep:
points: **Rivalry**: many equal competitors, slow growth, high fixed costs and price wars → low profits.
**New entrants**: low barriers (capital, brand, scale, licences, distribution) → new firms flood in.
**Substitutes**: products from *other* industries doing the same job (video calls vs business travel).
**Buyer power**: concentrated or price-sensitive buyers squeeze prices (large retailers vs FMCG makers).
**Supplier power**: a few critical suppliers capture profit (aircraft engines, chip makers).
Note: complements and government are factors that shift the forces, not forces themselves.

notes.h: Worked example: why Indian airlines struggle
notes.p: Take an illustrative airline with ₹10,000 crore revenue. Fuel (supplier power of oil markets) might be roughly 35–40% of costs; aircraft lessors and engine makers (few suppliers) take another big slice; passengers compare fares on apps (high buyer power, low switching cost); trains and Vande Bharat on short routes are substitutes; and rivals with high fixed costs cut prices to fill seats. Even if the airline earns, say, ₹10,500 crore and spends ₹10,200 crore, the margin is only about 3% (₹300 crore / ₹10,500 crore ≈ 2.9%) — one fuel spike wipes it out. All five forces are strong; that is why many Indian airlines (Kingfisher, Jet Airways) failed despite booming demand.

notes.h: Generic strategies and the value chain
notes.p:
**Cost leadership**: be the lowest-cost producer, e.g. D-Mart owning its stores, buying in bulk and paying suppliers fast in return for lower prices. **Differentiation**: be unique on something buyers value — Apple's design and ecosystem, Titan's trust and retail experience. **Focus**: serve a niche better — e.g. a cost focus on a single region or a differentiation focus on luxury.

The **value chain** is how you find the source of advantage. List every activity and ask: where do we have a cost edge, where do we create uniqueness? Asian Paints, for example, built an edge in outbound logistics and demand forecasting, letting dealers hold less stock while being restocked often.

notes.h: What Is Strategy? Trade-offs and fit
notes.p: In his 1996 HBR essay Porter attacked the 1990s fashion for TQM, benchmarking and reengineering. These improve **operational effectiveness**, but everyone can copy them, so gains are competed away to customers. **Strategy** is different: choose a distinctive set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value. That requires **trade-offs** — Southwest Airlines chose not to serve meals, assign seats or connect bags — and **fit**, where activities reinforce each other. A rival can copy one activity; copying an entire system is far harder.

In 'Creating Shared Value' (HBR, 2011, with Mark Kramer), Porter argued that social problems are business opportunities: reconceive products and markets (affordable health or finance), redefine productivity in the value chain (Nestlé's work with dairy farmers is their famous example), and build supportive industry clusters. Amul and ITC e-Choupal are often cited in India as shared-value-style models.

**Criticisms:** Five Forces is static — it struggles with fast-changing digital platforms where network effects and ecosystems matter more than industry boundaries. Generic strategies can be too rigid: Toyota and IKEA combine low cost with differentiation. Porter's own consulting firm, Monitor Group, went bankrupt in 2012, which critics enjoy pointing out. Shared value has been called 'CSR rebranded' by some scholars.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting case interviews expect a quick **industry attractiveness** read — Five Forces is the natural structure for 'Should our client enter the EV-charging business?' In exams, you'll be asked to apply Five Forces to an industry and identify the generic strategy of a firm. In real jobs, Porter's 'what will we NOT do?' is the most useful question in any strategy meeting.

points: **Five Forces**: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power (1979 HBR; *Competitive Strategy* 1980).
**Generic strategies**: cost leadership, differentiation, focus; avoid being **stuck in the middle**.
**Value chain** (*Competitive Advantage*, 1985): primary + support activities; source of cost or uniqueness.
**Operational effectiveness ≠ strategy** (1996): strategy = unique position + trade-offs + fit.
**Shared value** (2011, with Kramer): profit by solving social problems inside the core business.
Critique: static, pre-platform; hybrids like Toyota break the 'pick one' rule.

chapters.title: Clayton Christensen: disruption and jobs-to-be-done

cards.title: The innovator's dilemma
cards.body: Clayton Christensen (1952–2020), a Harvard professor, asked why **well-managed** leaders fail. His answer in *The Innovator's Dilemma* (1997): they fail precisely *because* they do the 'right' things — listen to best customers, chase higher margins, invest where returns look biggest. That rational behaviour makes them ignore cheap, inferior-looking new technologies until too late.

cards.title: Sustaining vs disruptive
cards.body: **Sustaining innovation** makes good products better for existing customers — incumbents usually win these races. **Disruptive innovation** starts with a product that is worse on traditional measures but **cheaper, simpler or more convenient**, aimed at overlooked customers. It then improves until it is good enough for the mainstream.

cards.title: Two types of disruption
cards.body: **Low-end disruption**: serves over-served customers with a 'good enough' cheaper product (mini-mills in steel making rebar first). **New-market disruption**: competes against **non-consumption** — people who couldn't use the product at all (personal computers vs mainframes; cheap smartphones bringing first-time internet users online).

cards.title: Why incumbents can't respond
cards.body: Christensen's **RPV** lens: a firm's **resources**, **processes** and **values** (its priorities — e.g. which margins are 'worth it') decide what it can do. A disruptive product offers low margins in a small market, so the values of a big firm reject it. Fix: create an **autonomous unit** with its own cost structure.

cards.title: Jobs-to-be-done
cards.body: In *Competing Against Luck* (2016) Christensen argued customers don't buy products; they **'hire' them to do a job** in a specific circumstance. The job has functional, emotional and social sides. Understand the job and you understand what you really compete with.

cards.title: The milkshake story
cards.body: A fast-food chain wanted to sell more milkshakes. Asking customers about flavours didn't help. Watching them revealed many bought shakes early morning for a **long, boring commute** — the job was 'keep me full and occupied with one hand'. The real competitors were bagels and bananas, not other shakes. Thicker shakes did the job better.

cards.title: Disruption is not just 'any big change'
cards.body: Christensen insisted the word be used precisely. In a 2015 HBR article he argued **Uber** was not disruptive in his sense — it didn't start at the low end or with non-consumers; it started with a product as good or better than taxis. Many 'disruptors' are just successful sustaining innovators.

cards.q: A new product that is cheaper and simpler, initially worse on mainstream metrics, and targets non-consumers is an example of:
cards.explain: Competing against non-consumption with a simpler, cheaper product is new-market disruption.

cards.q: In Christensen's view, why do well-run incumbents often miss disruption?
options: They rationally focus on best customers and higher margins
cards.explain: The dilemma is that good management — listening to profitable customers — is what blinds them.

cards.q: In the milkshake example, the main 'competitor' for the morning milkshake was:
options: Bagels, bananas and other commute snacks
cards.explain: Jobs-to-be-done shows competition is whatever else customers hire for the same job — here, boring-commute breakfast.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Clayton Christensen studied the hard-disk-drive industry in the 1990s and noticed a strange pattern: each new, smaller drive size (14-inch to 8 to 5.25 to 3.5) was led by **new entrants**, and the leaders of one generation were often wiped out in the next. The incumbents were not lazy or stupid. They listened carefully to their best customers, who did not want the smaller, lower-capacity drives at first. By the time the small drives were good enough, the entrants owned them.

That is the **innovator's dilemma**: the practices that make you excellent at serving today's customers can make you blind to tomorrow's market.

Picture two lines on a chart. One shows the performance customers can actually use; it rises slowly. The other shows the performance incumbents deliver through **sustaining innovation**; it rises faster, so eventually products **overshoot** what most customers need. That gap leaves room for an entrant with a simpler, cheaper product.
points: **Step 1**: entrant targets the low end or non-consumers with a 'worse' product; incumbent happily cedes this low-margin segment.
**Step 2**: the entrant improves along its own trajectory.
**Step 3**: once 'good enough' for mainstream customers, its cost or convenience edge wins.
**Step 4**: incumbent retreats up-market until little is left.
Examples Christensen used: steel mini-mills vs integrated mills, PCs vs minicomputers, discount retailers vs department stores.

notes.h: Why incumbents can't just respond: RPV
notes.p:
Christensen argued capabilities come from **resources** (people, cash, technology), **processes** (how work gets done) and **values** (the criteria for prioritising — e.g. 'we only pursue projects with 40% gross margins and ₹500 crore potential'). A disruptive opportunity fails those values every time.

**Worked example (illustrative numbers):** A large firm with ₹10,000 crore revenue targets 10% growth = ₹1,000 crore of new revenue a year. A disruptive product might bring ₹50 crore in year one at a 15% margin = ₹7.5 crore profit, versus its core 35% margin. To the board it is 5% of the growth target at less than half the margin — rationally rejected. An entrant with ₹20 crore revenue sees the same ₹50 crore as **2.5× growth**. Same opportunity, opposite verdicts. Christensen's remedy: put it in a separate unit whose size and values match the opportunity.

Christensen's second big idea: segment markets by the **job** customers are trying to get done, not by age, income or product category. A job has **functional** (fill me up), **emotional** (I feel less bored) and **social** (I look professional) dimensions, and arises in a **circumstance**.

India examples: UPI did not win because people wanted 'digital payments' in the abstract; the job was 'pay the chaiwala exactly, instantly, without change'. Many families 'hire' coaching institutes less for teaching than for the job of 'give my child structure and give me peace of mind'. When you see the job, competitors look different — a tuition app competes with the neighbourhood aunty's tuition, not just other apps.

**Global:** Netflix's DVD-by-mail and early streaming started worse than Blockbuster on immediacy and selection but served customers Blockbuster neglected; Kodak invented an early digital camera but its values were built around film margins. **India:** Jio's free voice and cheap data looked like a low-margin play to incumbents but created new-market demand among hundreds of millions of first-time data users. Low-cost smartphones from Chinese brands and later Indian assembly brought first-time users online — competing against non-consumption. Micro-finance and small-ticket insurance follow the same logic.

Historian Jill Lepore (New Yorker, 2014) argued Christensen's case selection was cherry-picked and that many 'disrupted' firms (like some disk-drive makers) survived. Researchers have found the theory predicts poorly ahead of time; it explains failures well in hindsight. The word 'disruption' also got diluted into a synonym for any innovation — Christensen himself pushed back, e.g. calling Uber not disruptive in his strict sense (HBR, 2015). And jobs-to-be-done can be vague in practice: two analysts can describe the same 'job' differently.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Product manager interviews love 'what job does this product do?' Consulting cases ask 'should the incumbent launch a cheaper brand?' — discuss cannibalisation, autonomous units and margin structure. In exams, define sustaining vs disruptive precisely and give one low-end and one new-market example.

points: *The Innovator's Dilemma* (1997): good management can cause failure.
**Sustaining** = better for existing customers; **disruptive** = cheaper/simpler, starts at low end or with non-consumers, improves upward.
Two types: **low-end** and **new-market** disruption.
**RPV**: resources, processes, values — values decide what a firm will fund.
Remedy: **autonomous unit** with fitting cost structure.
**Jobs-to-be-done** (*Competing Against Luck*, 2016): customers 'hire' products for a job in a circumstance; milkshake story.
Critique: hindsight bias, cherry-picked cases, term overused.

chapters.title: Deming & Ohno: quality, PDCA and the Toyota Way

cards.title: Two quality revolutionaries
cards.body: **W. Edwards Deming** (1900–1993), an American statistician, taught Japanese industry from 1950 that quality comes from managing **systems and variation**. **Taiichi Ohno** (1912–1990) built the **Toyota Production System (TPS)** — the basis of 'lean'. Together they explain why Japanese cars beat Detroit in the 1970s–80s.

cards.title: PDCA cycle
cards.body: **Plan** (define the problem and a hypothesis), **Do** (try it small), **Check** (measure — Deming preferred 'Study'), **Act** (standardise if it worked, else adjust). Derived from Walter Shewhart's work; Deming spread it. It is the scientific method applied to daily work, repeated endlessly — the engine of **kaizen** (continuous improvement).

cards.title: Common vs special causes
cards.body: Deming said most problems (he estimated the vast majority, often quoted as ~94%) come from the **system**, not workers. **Common-cause** variation is built into the process; **special-cause** variation comes from a specific event. Blaming people for common-cause variation is useless — management must change the system.

cards.title: The 14 points (highlights)
cards.body: From *Out of the Crisis* (1982): create **constancy of purpose**; cease dependence on mass inspection — build quality in; end awarding business on price alone; improve constantly; **drive out fear**; break down barriers between departments; **eliminate slogans and numerical quotas**; remove barriers to pride of workmanship.

cards.title: TPS: two pillars
cards.body: Ohno's system rests on **Just-in-Time** (make only what is needed, when needed, in the amount needed — pulled by **kanban** cards) and **jidoka** (automation with a human touch: stop the line when a defect appears, e.g. pulling the **andon** cord). Goal: eliminate **muda** (waste).

cards.title: The seven wastes
cards.body: Ohno's list of muda: **overproduction** (the worst), **waiting**, **transport**, **over-processing**, **inventory**, **motion**, **defects**. Lean thinkers later added an eighth: unused human talent. Each is a cost the customer doesn't pay for.

cards.title: Little's Law: why inventory slows you
cards.body: **Lead time = Work-in-progress ÷ Throughput.** A plant with 600 units of WIP finishing 100 units/day has a 6-day lead time. Cut WIP to 200 and lead time drops to 2 days — same capacity, faster response, defects found sooner. This is why lean attacks inventory.

cards.q: In PDCA, what should you do in the 'Act' step if the trial worked?
options: Standardise the change and roll it out
cards.explain: Act = adopt and standardise what worked (or adjust and re-cycle if it didn't).

cards.q: Which of these is one of Toyota's two pillars of TPS?
cards.explain: TPS rests on Just-in-Time and jidoka (stopping to fix defects at source).

cards.q: A line has WIP of 450 units and throughput of 150 units/day. What is the lead time?
cards.explain: Little's Law: 450 ÷ 150 = 3 days.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
After World War II, Japanese goods were seen as cheap and shoddy. Within about three decades Toyota, Sony and others became the global benchmark for quality. Two people are central to that story. **W. Edwards Deming**, an American statistician, lectured Japanese executives from 1950 on statistical quality control; Japan named its top quality award the **Deming Prize**. **Taiichi Ohno**, a Toyota engineer, spent decades building the **Toyota Production System**, inspired partly by how American supermarkets restock shelves only as items are taken.

The shared idea: **quality and efficiency come from the system, not from inspecting and blaming people.** Build quality in, reduce variation, eliminate waste, and improve a little every day.

notes.h: Deming: variation, PDCA and the 14 points
notes.p:
Deming's foundation is **variation**. Every process varies. **Common-cause** variation is the natural noise of the system; **special-cause** variation has an identifiable source (a bad batch, a broken tool). Control charts tell you which you are looking at. Reacting to common-cause noise as if it were special ('tampering') makes things worse.

His improvement engine is **PDCA**: Plan, Do, Check (he preferred Study), Act. His famous **red bead experiment** made the point vividly: workers scooping beads from a box with a fixed share of red 'defects' got different results by pure chance, yet were praised or fired — absurd, because the system decided the outcome.

The **14 points** in *Out of the Crisis* (1982) include constancy of purpose, ending mass inspection, ending purchase on price alone, constant improvement, training, leadership instead of supervision, **driving out fear**, removing barriers between departments, and eliminating slogans, quotas and management by numerical targets.
Ohno's TPS (described in his book *Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production*, 1978) has two pillars:
points: **Just-in-Time**: produce only what the next process needs. Downstream 'pulls' work using **kanban** signals instead of upstream 'pushing' to a forecast.
**Jidoka**: machines and people stop when something is wrong, so defects are fixed at source. Any worker can pull the **andon** cord.
**Heijunka**: level the production mix so demand on upstream steps is smooth.
**Standard work** + **kaizen**: write down the current best way, then improve it.
**5 Whys**: ask 'why?' repeatedly to reach the root cause, not the symptom.
Target: the **seven wastes** — overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, inventory, motion, defects.

notes.h: Worked example: lean in an Indian auto-parts plant
notes.p:
An illustrative Pune supplier makes brake assemblies. WIP on the floor is 1,200 units; the line ships 300 a day. By Little's Law, lead time = 1,200 ÷ 300 = **4 days**. A defect introduced at step 1 might not be caught for four days — by then 1,200 suspect units exist.

After introducing kanban with a cap of 300 units of WIP: lead time = 300 ÷ 300 = **1 day**. If each unit carries about ₹2,000 of material, working capital tied up in WIP falls from ₹24 lakh (1,200 × ₹2,000) to ₹6 lakh (300 × ₹2,000) — ₹18 lakh freed — and defects surface within a day. Maruti Suzuki's tie-up with Suzuki in the 1980s brought exactly these Japanese practices to Indian suppliers; many Indian firms (e.g. Sundaram-Clayton in the TVS group) went on to win the Deming Prize, and India has been one of the largest sources of Deming Prize winners outside Japan.

Lean has spread far beyond cars. Hospitals use it to cut patient waiting (Aravind Eye Care in India is famous for an assembly-line-like flow that keeps cost per surgery very low). Software borrowed it: **Lean Startup** (Eric Ries) applies build-measure-learn, a PDCA cousin; **Kanban boards** in Agile come straight from Toyota. Amazon's fulfilment centres use andon-like stop mechanisms. The **Toyota Way** (codified internally around 2001 and popularised by Jeffrey Liker's 2004 book) adds two values: **continuous improvement** and **respect for people**.

Firms copy the tools (kanban boards, 5S posters) without the **philosophy** — respect for people and patient problem-solving — and get little result. Running inventory too lean leaves supply chains brittle: the 2011 Japan earthquake and the 2020–22 chip shortage showed JIT's fragility, and Toyota itself began holding buffers of critical parts. Deming's anti-target stance is hard to square with modern KPI cultures. And lean cost-cutting can become a euphemism for layoffs, which destroys the trust that kaizen needs.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Operations interviews often ask you to find waste in a process or apply Little's Law. Consulting cases on manufacturing or hospitals use lean language — bottleneck, WIP, cycle time. Exams test PDCA steps, the seven wastes and the two pillars of TPS. In any job, '5 Whys' is the fastest way to stop fixing symptoms.

points: **Deming**: quality comes from the system; common vs special cause variation; ~most problems are the system's.
**PDCA** (Plan-Do-Check/Study-Act), from Shewhart; engine of **kaizen**.
**14 points** (*Out of the Crisis*, 1982): constancy of purpose, drive out fear, no slogans/quotas, build quality in.
**Ohno's TPS**: pillars = **Just-in-Time** (pull, kanban) + **jidoka** (stop and fix; andon).
**Seven wastes**: overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, inventory, motion, defects.
**Little's Law**: lead time = WIP ÷ throughput.
Toyota Way = continuous improvement + respect for people.
Critique: tools without philosophy fail; JIT can be fragile.

chapters.title: Buffett & Munger: moats, margin of safety and mental models

cards.title: Two investors, many management lessons
cards.body: **Warren Buffett** (born 1930) turned Berkshire Hathaway, a failing textile mill, into one of the world's largest companies. His partner **Charlie Munger** (1924–2023) shaped his thinking. Their ideas — moats, circles of competence, margin of safety, mental models — are now core to strategy, not just investing. Buffett handed the CEO role to Greg Abel from 2026.

cards.title: Economic moat
cards.body: A **moat** is a durable advantage that protects a business's high returns from competitors, like a moat around a castle. Sources: **brand** (Coca-Cola, Fevicol), **network effects**, **switching costs**, **cost advantages/scale**, **regulatory licences**. Test: can it earn high returns on capital for many years despite rivals trying?

cards.title: Circle of competence
cards.body: Know what you understand well — and, more importantly, **where its boundary is**. Buffett famously avoided most tech stocks for decades because he couldn't predict their economics. The size of the circle matters less than knowing its edge. Managers apply it to acquisitions and diversification.

cards.title: Margin of safety
cards.body:
From Buffett's teacher **Benjamin Graham**: buy only when price is well below your estimate of intrinsic value.
**Margin of safety = (Value − Price) ÷ Value.**
Value ₹1,000, price ₹700 → (1,000 − 700) ÷ 1,000 = **30%**. The cushion absorbs errors in your estimate and bad luck.

cards.title: Mr. Market
cards.body: Graham's parable: imagine a manic-depressive partner, Mr. Market, who offers daily to buy or sell your share of the business at wildly varying prices. You are free to ignore him. Use his mood swings; never take his price as information about value.

cards.title: Munger's mental models
cards.body: Munger urged a **latticework of mental models** from many disciplines — compound interest, incentives, opportunity cost, psychology, evolution, engineering redundancy. One-model thinkers are like 'a man with a hammer', to whom every problem looks like a nail.

cards.title: Inversion
cards.body: Munger borrowed from mathematician Jacobi: **'Invert, always invert.'** Instead of asking 'how do we succeed?', ask 'what would guarantee failure?' and avoid it. A manager planning a launch lists ways it could die (stock-outs, bad reviews, a price war), then designs against each.

cards.q: Intrinsic value is estimated at ₹500 per share; the market price is ₹400. What is the margin of safety?
cards.explain: (500 − 400) ÷ 500 = 0.20 = 20%. Note it is measured against value, not price.

cards.q: Which is the best example of a moat from switching costs?
options: Core banking software that a bank would find painful and risky to replace
A new restaurant with good food
cards.explain: Replacing deeply embedded software is costly and risky, locking customers in — a classic switching-cost moat.

cards.q: 'Invert, always invert' means:
options: Think about what would cause failure and avoid it
Turn the org chart upside down
cards.explain: Inversion approaches a problem backwards — identify what to avoid.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Buffett and Munger are investors, but MBA programmes teach them because they think like **owners of whole businesses**. Their question is always: will this business earn high returns on the capital it uses, for a long time, and am I paying a sensible price for it? That question applies just as much to a CEO allocating capital between projects as to a fund manager picking stocks.

Buffett studied under **Benjamin Graham** at Columbia; Graham's books *Security Analysis* (1934, with David Dodd) and *The Intelligent Investor* (1949) gave him margin of safety and Mr. Market. Munger pushed Buffett beyond buying 'cheap, mediocre businesses' toward buying **wonderful businesses at fair prices** — the See's Candies purchase in 1972 was the turning point.

notes.h: Idea 1: Moats and return on capital
notes.p:
A good business turns a rupee of capital into a lot of profit, year after year. Competition normally destroys this: high returns attract rivals, prices fall, returns drift down. A **moat** stops that.

**Worked example (illustrative):** Business A needs ₹100 crore of capital and earns ₹25 crore after-tax operating profit: return on capital **25%**. Business B needs the same ₹100 crore and earns ₹8 crore: **8%**. If both reinvest all profits at the same returns for 10 years, A's capital compounds to about ₹100 × 1.25¹⁰ ≈ **₹931 crore** while B's grows to ₹100 × 1.08¹⁰ ≈ **₹216 crore**. The moat is what lets A keep earning 25% instead of being dragged to the average.

Indian moats: **Asian Paints** (dealer network and tinting/logistics systems), **Pidilite** (Fevicol is almost a generic word for adhesive), **HDFC Bank** (low-cost deposit franchise), stock exchanges and depositories (network effects + regulation).

notes.h: Idea 2: Circle of competence and margin of safety
notes.p:
**Circle of competence**: be honest about what you truly understand. Buffett's 1999 refusal to join the dot-com boom looked foolish for a year, then wise. For a manager, it means saying no to diversifications the team can't evaluate — a cement company buying a fintech startup, say.

**Margin of safety**: your estimate of value will be wrong; build in a cushion. If you think a plant acquisition is worth ₹400 crore based on cash flows, don't pay ₹390 crore — pay ₹280–300 crore or walk away. At ₹300 crore the margin is (400 − 300) ÷ 400 = **25%**. Engineers do the same when they design a bridge for loads well above what they expect.

notes.h: Idea 3: Mental models, incentives and inversion
notes.p:
Munger's 1995 talk 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' listed about two dozen tendencies that lead people astray — incentive-caused bias, social proof, commitment and consistency, envy, deprival-superreaction and more. His advice: carry a **latticework** of the big ideas from many fields and check decisions against them.

His favourite: **incentives**. He is widely quoted as saying 'Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome.' If sales reps are paid on volume, expect discounts and bad-credit customers. If loan officers are paid on disbursal, expect NPAs later.

**Inversion**: before a decision, ask how it could fail. Pre-mortems in modern companies (imagine it is a year later and the project failed — why?) are inversion in practice.

Capital allocation is the CEO's most important job, Buffett argues in his shareholder letters: reinvest in the business, acquire, pay dividends, or buy back shares — choose whichever earns the most per rupee. He praises managers who think like owners and criticises 'institutional imperative' — copying peers' acquisitions and expansions just because they are doing it.

Berkshire's own structure is a lesson in **decentralisation and trust**: a tiny head office, subsidiaries run by their own CEOs with little interference, and capital allocated centrally.

Buffett's approach is hard to copy: his scale, cheap 'float' from insurance and reputation give him deals others can't get. Moats in technology can vanish fast (Nokia, BlackBerry), which is why he long avoided tech — though Berkshire later made a huge, very successful bet on Apple. Mental-model lists can become trivia collections rather than real judgement. And 'buy great businesses and hold forever' can leave you holding businesses whose moats quietly eroded — newspapers were once Buffett's favourite moat.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: In finance and consulting interviews: 'Does this company have a moat? What is it?' — name the type and the evidence (high ROCE sustained over years, pricing power). In strategy exams, moats tie neatly to Porter's barriers to entry. In real jobs, inversion and pre-mortems are some of the most practical tools you'll ever use.

points: Graham → Buffett: **margin of safety** = (Value − Price) ÷ Value; **Mr. Market** is a servant, not a guide.
**Moat** = durable advantage protecting high returns: brand, network effects, switching costs, cost/scale, licences.
Moats show up as **high return on capital sustained** for years.
**Circle of competence**: know its boundary.
Munger: **latticework of mental models**; beware the man with a hammer.
**Incentives** drive behaviour; **inversion** — ask what causes failure.
Capital allocation is the CEO's key job; avoid the institutional imperative.
Critique: hard to copy, tech moats fragile, mental models can become trivia.

chapters.title: Andy Grove: High Output Management, OKRs and paranoia

cards.title: Who was Andy Grove?
cards.body: Andy Grove (1936–2016) escaped Hungary as a refugee in 1956, became one of Intel's earliest employees at its 1968 founding, and was CEO from 1987 to 1998. He led Intel's exit from memory chips into microprocessors. His books *High Output Management* (1983) and *Only the Paranoid Survive* (1996) remain favourites of tech founders.

cards.title: A manager's output
cards.body: Grove's definition: **a manager's output = the output of their organisation + the output of neighbouring organisations under their influence.** Not your emails or meetings — your team's results. So a manager's job is choosing activities with the highest **leverage**.

cards.title: Managerial leverage
cards.body: Leverage = output generated per unit of your activity. High-leverage actions: a one-hour training session that improves ten people for a year; a decision that unblocks a team; a timely 'no'. Low leverage: doing work your team should do, or meddling in details. Every manager has the same 24 hours; leverage decides output.

cards.title: The breakfast factory
cards.body: Grove explained production with a breakfast of boiled egg, toast and coffee. Schedule around the **limiting step** (the 4-minute egg); catch defects at the **lowest-value stage** (check the egg before plating, not after serving); and decide where to hold **inventory**. These principles apply to any team's work.

cards.title: OKRs
cards.body: Grove adapted Drucker's MBO at Intel into **Objectives and Key Results**: an **Objective** says *what* you want (qualitative, inspiring); 2–5 **Key Results** say *how you'll know* (measurable, time-bound). John Doerr, who worked at Intel, took OKRs to Google in 1999; they spread across Silicon Valley and Indian startups.

cards.title: An OKR that works
cards.body: **Objective:** Make our app the easiest way for Pune college students to pay hostel fees. **KRs:** (1) 40% of partner hostels accept payments by Dec; (2) payment completes in < 30 seconds for 95% of users; (3) support tickets per 1,000 payments fall from 12 to 4. Note: outcomes, not tasks like 'build a feature'.

cards.title: Strategic inflection points
cards.body: In *Only the Paranoid Survive*, a **strategic inflection point** is when a **'10× force'** changes an industry's fundamentals. Intel faced one in the mid-1980s as Japanese firms crushed memory prices. Grove asked Gordon Moore: if the board brought in a new CEO, what would he do? 'Get out of memories.' So they did it themselves.

cards.q: By Grove's definition, a manager's output is:
options: The number of hours they work
Their team's output plus that of neighbouring teams they influence
cards.explain: Grove measured managers by the output of the organisations they lead and influence.

cards.q: Which is the best Key Result?
options: Raise 30-day retention from 25% to 35% by March
cards.explain: Key results should be measurable outcomes with a deadline, not activities or vague intentions.

cards.q: Intel's exit from memory chips is Grove's example of:
cards.explain: A 10× force (Japanese competition) changed memory economics — a strategic inflection point that demanded a new strategy.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Andy Grove brought an engineer's mind to management. He believed management is a **production process**: inputs (your time, information, decisions) produce outputs (your team's results). If you treat it that way, you can measure it, find bottlenecks and improve it. He also believed the biggest danger to a successful company is **complacency**, hence his title *Only the Paranoid Survive*.

Grove was a Hungarian refugee who arrived in the US in 1956, earned a PhD in chemical engineering, joined Intel at its 1968 founding alongside Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, and was CEO from 1987 to 1998. *Time* named him Man of the Year in 1997.

notes.h: Idea 1: Output, leverage and the breakfast factory
notes.p:
**Manager's output = output of their organisation + output of neighbouring organisations under their influence.** This makes a manager's day a resource-allocation problem.

**Worked example of leverage (illustrative):** You manage 8 analysts. Option A: you personally build a report — 6 hours, one report. Option B: you spend 3 hours writing a template and 1 hour training the team; each analyst then saves 1 hour a week. Over 20 weeks that is 8 × 1 × 20 = **160 hours** saved for 4 hours of your time — leverage of 40×. Grove would pick B every time.

The **breakfast factory** teaches production principles: build the schedule around the **limiting step**; detect defects at the **lowest-value stage** (incoming inspection is cheaper than a customer complaint); and use **indicators** that predict trouble early. He also recommended pairing indicators so you don't over-optimise one (measure both inventory and stock-outs).

notes.h: Idea 2: One-on-ones, meetings and task-relevant maturity
notes.p:
Grove made the **one-on-one** a standard practice: a regular meeting owned by the *subordinate*, where they bring the agenda and the manager listens, coaches and learns about problems early. He divided meetings into **process-oriented** (regular, like staff meetings) and **mission-oriented** (to make a specific decision).

**Task-relevant maturity**: how you manage depends on how experienced the person is *at this specific task*. Low maturity → structured, telling. Medium → more two-way, focused on the individual. High → monitor objectives only. The same senior engineer might need close guidance on her first client negotiation.
Grove adapted MBO into what became **OKRs**. Rules of thumb that came out of Intel and Google practice:
points: Objectives: few (3–5), qualitative, ambitious.
Key Results: 2–5 per objective, **measurable outcomes**, with a date.
Set **quarterly**; often aligned up and down but not all cascaded top-down.
Stretch goals: at Google, scoring about 0.6–0.7 on a 0–1 scale was considered healthy for ambitious OKRs.
Keep OKRs separate from compensation, so people set bold goals honestly.
Make them visible across the company.

notes.h: Idea 4: Strategic inflection points and constructive confrontation
notes.p:
A **strategic inflection point** happens when the balance of forces shifts from the old structure to a new one — a '10× force' in competition, technology, customers, suppliers, complementors or regulation. Signals are noisy at first; middle managers in the field often see them before the CEO.

Intel's case: by the mid-1980s Japanese manufacturers were producing memory chips at quality and prices Intel couldn't match. In 1985 Grove asked Moore what a new CEO would do; Moore answered: get out of memories. They exited and bet the company on microprocessors — the foundation of Intel's dominance in the PC era.

Grove also championed **constructive confrontation**: attack problems, not people, and argue hard regardless of rank. In 1994, he learned the costly lesson of the **Pentium FDIV bug**: Intel's engineers judged the floating-point flaw statistically rare, but customers felt they deserved a replacement; Intel eventually offered replacements and took a large charge.

notes.h: Applying Grove today — India and global
notes.p: Google, LinkedIn and many Indian startups (including fintech and SaaS firms) run on OKRs. Indian IT services majors faced their own inflection point with generative AI: when a 10× force makes code generation cheap, the old billing-by-headcount model is under threat — Grove would say listen to the 'Cassandras' in delivery teams, run experiments, then commit decisively. Telecom operators faced one when Jio's 2016 entry turned voice into a near-free product.

OKRs often degrade into **task lists**, too many objectives, or a bureaucratic cascade. Tied to bonuses, they invite sandbagging. 'Paranoia' can become a culture of fear or permanent crisis. And Intel itself later missed big inflection points — mobile chips (it passed on supplying the original iPhone) and leading-edge manufacturing — showing how hard Grove's own advice is to follow.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Tech, product and consulting interviews often ask you to write OKRs for a business or critique a set of goals — keep objectives qualitative and key results measurable. Strategy exams use Intel's memory exit as the standard example of a strategic inflection point. In your first managerial job, Grove's one-on-ones and leverage test ('what is the highest-output use of my next hour?') are immediately usable.

points: Grove: Intel employee at founding (1968), CEO 1987–98; *High Output Management* (1983), *Only the Paranoid Survive* (1996).
**Manager's output** = output of own org + neighbouring orgs influenced.
Choose **high-leverage** activities; breakfast factory: limiting step, catch defects early.
**One-on-ones** are owned by the subordinate; **task-relevant maturity** sets management style.
**OKRs**: qualitative Objective + 2–5 measurable Key Results; Doerr took them to Google (1999).
**Strategic inflection point** = 10× force; Intel's 1985 exit from memories.
Critique: OKRs become task lists; Intel later missed mobile.

chapters.title: Jim Collins: Good to Great, Level 5 and the flywheel

cards.title: Research-based leadership books
cards.body: Jim Collins, a former Stanford lecturer, writes books built on comparing matched pairs of companies. *Built to Last* (1994, with Jerry Porras) studied enduring visionary firms; *Good to Great* (2001) studied 11 companies that jumped from average to great results and **sustained** it for 15 years, versus similar firms that didn't.

cards.title: Level 5 leadership
cards.body: The good-to-great CEOs were not celebrity heroes. They combined **personal humility** with **intense professional will**. They credit others when things go well ('the window') and blame themselves when they go badly ('the mirror'). Charismatic egos often helped companies decline.

cards.title: First who, then what
cards.body: Great leaders first got the **right people on the bus** (and the wrong people off, and the right people in the right seats) — then figured out where to drive it. If you have the right people, the problem of motivating and managing them largely goes away.

cards.title: The Stockdale paradox
cards.body: Named after Admiral James Stockdale, a POW for years: retain **unwavering faith** that you will prevail in the end, *and* confront the **most brutal facts** of your current reality. Optimists who expected rescue 'by Christmas' broke; realistic believers survived.

cards.title: The hedgehog concept
cards.body: The fox knows many things; the hedgehog knows one big thing. Find the intersection of three circles: what you are **deeply passionate** about, what you can be **best in the world** at, and what drives your **economic engine** — one key ratio, **'profit per X'** (e.g. Walgreens: profit per customer visit).

cards.title: The flywheel vs the doom loop
cards.body: Greatness doesn't come from one dramatic launch. It comes from pushing a heavy **flywheel** consistently — each turn builds on the last until momentum takes over. Firms in the **doom loop** lurch from one programme, acquisition or saviour CEO to the next. Amazon famously drew its own flywheel.

cards.title: Built to Last ideas
cards.body: Visionary companies are **clock builders, not time tellers** — they build institutions that outlast any leader. They **preserve the core** (values, purpose) and **stimulate progress** (BHAGs — Big Hairy Audacious Goals). They embrace the **'genius of the AND'** over the 'tyranny of the OR'.

cards.q: Collins's Level 5 leader is best described as:
cards.explain: Level 5 = personal humility + professional will.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of the three circles of the hedgehog concept?
options: What you are deeply passionate about
What your largest competitor is doing
What you can be best in the world at
cards.explain: The hedgehog ignores competitor-chasing; it focuses on passion, best-in-world, and the economic engine.

cards.q: The Stockdale paradox asks leaders to:
options: Avoid bad news to keep morale up
Keep faith in eventual success while confronting brutal facts
cards.explain: Faith in the end + brutal honesty about the present.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Jim Collins asks: what separates companies that become and stay great from comparable ones that don't? His method is to pick firms with exceptional results, match each with a similar company in the same industry that did *not* achieve them, and look for the differences. In *Good to Great* (2001) his team screened Fortune 500 companies for a pattern of 15 years at or below market returns followed by 15 years of cumulative returns at least three times the market, and found 11.

The surprising findings: greatness came less from strategy brilliance or technology than from **disciplined people, disciplined thought and disciplined action**, accumulated steadily.

notes.h: The Good to Great framework in detail
points: **Level 5 leadership**: humility + will; window and mirror.
**First who, then what**: right people on the bus before deciding direction.
**Confront the brutal facts** (Stockdale paradox): create a climate where truth is heard.
**Hedgehog concept**: passion ∩ best in world ∩ economic engine ('profit per X').
**Culture of discipline**: freedom within a framework; a 'stop doing' list.
**Technology accelerators**: technology accelerates momentum but does not create it.
**Flywheel**: cumulative, consistent effort; avoid the doom loop.
Later book *How the Mighty Fall* (2009): five stages of decline — hubris born of success, undisciplined pursuit of more, denial of risk, grasping for salvation, capitulation.

notes.h: Worked example: finding your 'profit per X'
notes.p: Collins's insight is that choosing the *right denominator* reveals your economic engine. Take an illustrative Indian value retailer with 300 stores, revenue ₹30,000 crore and operating profit ₹2,400 crore.
points: Profit per store = ₹2,400 ÷ 300 = **₹8 crore**.
If average store size is 40,000 sq ft, total = 1.2 crore sq ft; revenue per sq ft = ₹30,000 crore ÷ 1.2 crore = **₹25,000 per sq ft per year**.
Profit per sq ft = ₹2,400 crore ÷ 1.2 crore = **₹2,000**.

If management chose 'revenue per store' as its metric, it might open huge stores in prime malls. Choosing 'profit per sq ft' instead pushes toward owned, efficient stores with fast-moving products — a sharper hedgehog. D-Mart's well-known focus on owning stores and high sales per square foot reflects this kind of thinking.

notes.p:
*Built to Last* (1994, with Jerry Porras) compared visionary companies (e.g. 3M, Sony, Walt Disney, Johnson & Johnson) with comparison firms. Key ideas: **clock building** — build an organisation that keeps telling the time after the founder is gone; a **core ideology** (values + purpose) that stays fixed while strategies change; **BHAGs** — bold 10–30-year goals like putting a man on the moon; and the **genius of the AND** — profit and purpose, stability and change.

**Indian lens:** the Tata group's long-standing values and trust ownership are a clock-building example; ISRO's lunar and Mars missions function as national BHAGs; Infosys's early dream of being a globally respected Indian company was a BHAG for a 1981 startup.

The **flywheel** became famous when Jeff Bezos sketched Amazon's: lower prices → more customer visits → more third-party sellers → wider selection → better customer experience → more growth → lower cost structure → lower prices. Each push strengthens the next.

For a manager: write your team's flywheel as a loop of 4–6 steps; agree your 'profit per X'; and keep a **stop-doing list**. Hiring is the most Collins-ian decision you make — 'when in doubt, don't hire; keep looking'.

The most famous critique: several 'great' companies stumbled soon after publication. **Circuit City** went bankrupt in 2009, and **Fannie Mae** needed a government rescue in 2008. Phil Rosenzweig's *The Halo Effect* (2007) argued that studies like this suffer from **survivorship bias** and the **halo effect** — when a firm does well, observers describe its culture and leaders as brilliant; when it fails, the same traits look like arrogance. Correlation is not causation, and data drawn from interviews and press articles inherits this halo. Collins responds that his principles describe what companies did *during* their great period, not a guarantee forever.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Leadership and OB exams test Level 5, hedgehog and flywheel; always add the halo-effect critique for full marks. In interviews, 'Who is a leader you admire?' is a chance to describe humility plus will. In general management roles, defining a single economic denominator is a powerful way to align a team.

points: *Built to Last* (1994, with Porras); *Good to Great* (2001); *How the Mighty Fall* (2009).
**Level 5**: humility + will; window and mirror.
**First who, then what**: right people on the bus.
**Stockdale paradox**: faith + brutal facts.
**Hedgehog**: passion ∩ best in world ∩ economic engine (**profit per X**).
**Flywheel** vs **doom loop**; Amazon's flywheel.
Clock building, core ideology, **BHAGs**, genius of the AND.
Critique: **halo effect**, survivorship bias; Circuit City, Fannie Mae.

chapters.title: Kahneman, Thaler and behavioural economics for managers

cards.title: Humans are not perfectly rational
cards.body: Psychologists **Daniel Kahneman** (1934–2024) and **Amos Tversky** showed people make **systematic, predictable** errors. Kahneman won the 2002 economics Nobel (Tversky had died in 1996). Economist **Richard Thaler** (Nobel 2017) built behavioural economics. For managers: your forecasts, hiring and pricing are biased — in predictable ways.

cards.title: System 1 and System 2
cards.body: From *Thinking, Fast and Slow* (2011): **System 1** is fast, automatic, intuitive (reading a face, 2 + 2). **System 2** is slow, effortful, logical (17 × 24). System 1 runs most of life and is usually fine — but it jumps to conclusions, and lazy System 2 often endorses them.

cards.title: Heuristics and biases
cards.body: **Anchoring**: an initial number pulls estimates toward it. **Availability**: we judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. **Representativeness**: we judge by resemblance and ignore base rates. **Overconfidence** and the **planning fallacy**: projects take longer and cost more than planned.

cards.title: Prospect theory and loss aversion
cards.body: Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 prospect theory: people judge outcomes as **gains or losses relative to a reference point**, and **losses hurt about twice as much** as equal gains please. So people reject a 50-50 bet to win or lose ₹1,000, and often take bigger risks to avoid a sure loss.

cards.title: Framing and sunk costs
cards.body: The same facts framed differently change choices: '90% survival' feels better than '10% mortality'. **Sunk cost fallacy**: continuing a failing project because of money already spent. Rational rule: only **future** costs and benefits matter.

cards.title: Nudges and choice architecture
cards.body: Thaler and Cass Sunstein's *Nudge* (2008): small changes in how choices are presented — especially **defaults** — change behaviour a lot without banning options. Automatic enrolment into retirement savings dramatically raises participation. Thaler's 'Save More Tomorrow' (with Shlomo Benartzi) commits future pay rises to saving.

cards.title: A nudge in India
cards.body: The 2015 **'Give It Up'** campaign asked better-off households to voluntarily surrender their LPG subsidy, using public appeals and social proof (lists of people who had given up). Millions did. It shows how **social norms** and easy opt-outs can move behaviour without mandates.

cards.q: A manager keeps funding a failing product 'because we've already spent ₹5 crore on it'. This is:
cards.explain: Past spending is sunk; only future costs and benefits should drive the decision.

cards.q: Prospect theory says losses are felt roughly:
options: Half as strongly as equal gains
Only when they exceed 10% of wealth
About twice as strongly as equal gains
cards.explain: Loss aversion estimates are typically around 2 — losses loom about twice as large.

cards.q: Making pension enrolment automatic with an opt-out is an example of:
cards.explain: Changing the default option is the classic nudge in choice architecture.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Traditional economics assumes people are rational: they weigh all information, know what they want and choose the best option. Kahneman and Tversky, starting in the 1970s, ran simple experiments showing that people deviate from rationality in **systematic** ways — the same errors, in the same direction, again and again. That means the errors can be predicted, and designed around.

For managers this matters everywhere: forecasts are overconfident, interviews are anchored by first impressions, pricing decisions are framed by last year's number, and failing projects survive because of sunk costs.

notes.h: The model: two systems and their biases
notes.p: **System 1** is fast, associative, emotional and always on. **System 2** is slow, deliberate and lazy — it checks System 1 only when it must. Kahneman's acronym **WYSIATI** ('what you see is all there is') captures System 1's habit of building a confident story from whatever little information is at hand.
points: **Anchoring**: in negotiations the first number pulls the final deal toward it.
**Availability**: after a news story about a fraud, managers overestimate fraud risk.
**Representativeness / base-rate neglect**: 'He looks like a great salesman' ignores that most new hires in that role leave within a year.
**Overconfidence & planning fallacy**: the inside view ignores how similar projects went.
**Confirmation bias**: seeking evidence for what we already believe.
**Halo effect**: one good trait colours the whole judgement.
**Loss aversion & endowment effect** (Thaler): we value what we own more than identical things we don't.

notes.h: Worked example: loss aversion and the planning fallacy
notes.p:
**Loss aversion.** Offer a manager a project with a 50% chance of +₹1 crore profit and a 50% chance of −₹1 crore loss. Expected value = 0.5 × 1 + 0.5 × (−1) = **₹0**. With a loss-aversion coefficient of about 2, the *felt* value is 0.5 × 1 − 0.5 × 2 × 1 = **−₹0.5 crore**, so they reject it. To make it feel neutral, the upside must be about **₹2 crore**. Across a company, this makes managers turn down many positive-expected-value bets — one reason firms under-invest in innovation.

**Planning fallacy.** A team estimates an ERP rollout at 9 months and ₹6 crore. Kahneman recommends the **outside view** (reference-class forecasting): look at similar projects. If past rollouts ran on average 40% over time and 30% over budget, the outside-view estimate is 9 × 1.4 = **12.6 months** and 6 × 1.3 = **₹7.8 crore**. Budget against that, not the optimistic plan.

Richard Thaler added **mental accounting** (people treat money differently depending on its mental 'account' — a festival bonus is spent more freely than salary), the **endowment effect**, and the idea of **nudges**. With Cass Sunstein, *Nudge* (2008) argued for **libertarian paternalism**: design the choice environment to help people make better choices while leaving them free to choose otherwise.

Tools: **defaults**, **simplification**, **social norms**, **timely reminders**, **commitment devices**. The UK set up a Behavioural Insights Team in 2010 and many governments followed; in India, NITI Aayog has worked on behavioural insights, and campaigns such as Swachh Bharat and 'Give It Up' used social norms heavily.

notes.h: How managers use it — Indian and global
notes.p: **Pricing:** a ₹999 price, a decoy 'medium' option that makes 'large' look like value, or showing a strikethrough MRP anchor. **HR:** structured interviews and scoring each candidate on the same criteria before discussion reduce halo and anchoring. **Decisions:** Kahneman's advice includes pre-mortems, independent estimates before group discussion, and checklists. **Product:** auto-renew subscriptions and default tips on food apps are nudges — powerful and ethically sensitive. In *Noise* (2021, with Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein), Kahneman added that random scatter in judgements — e.g. two underwriters quoting very different premiums for the same risk — is as costly as bias.

Using behavioural tricks to exploit customers ('dark patterns' — hidden opt-outs, fake countdown timers) crosses into manipulation and attracts regulators; India's consumer authority issued guidelines against dark patterns in 2023. Some famous priming findings in the field failed to replicate, and Kahneman himself acknowledged that parts of the priming chapter in his book relied on weak studies. Nudges often have **small** effects at scale, and critics argue they distract from harder structural reforms.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Marketing and product interviews ask you to design a nudge or explain pricing psychology. OB and decision-making exams test named biases with short scenarios — identify the bias, then propose a debiasing tool. In consulting and finance, citing the outside view when a client's forecast looks rosy is a mark of maturity.

points: Kahneman & Tversky: **heuristics and biases**; prospect theory (1979); Nobel 2002 (Kahneman).
**System 1** fast/intuitive, **System 2** slow/deliberate; WYSIATI.
Biases: anchoring, availability, representativeness, overconfidence, planning fallacy, confirmation, halo.
**Loss aversion** ≈ 2×; reference points; framing.
**Sunk costs** are irrelevant — only future matters.
Thaler (Nobel 2017): mental accounting, endowment effect, **Nudge** (2008, with Sunstein), defaults.
Debiasing: outside view, pre-mortem, structured interviews, independent estimates.
Critique: replication issues, small effects, risk of dark patterns.

chapters.title: C.K. Prahalad: core competence and the bottom of the pyramid

cards.title: An Indian-born strategy giant
cards.body: C.K. Prahalad (1941–2010) grew up in Tamil Nadu, worked at Union Carbide in India, did his doctorate at Harvard and taught at the University of Michigan. Two big ideas: **core competence** (with Gary Hamel, HBR 1990) and **The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid** (2004). He was regularly ranked among the world's most influential management thinkers.

cards.title: Core competence
cards.body: A **core competence** is the collective learning of an organisation — a bundle of skills and technologies — especially how to coordinate diverse production skills. It is not a product or a business unit. Think of **Honda's engines**, **Canon's optics and imaging**, **Sony's miniaturisation**: each powered many different products.

cards.title: Three tests
cards.body: A true core competence (1) gives **access to a wide variety of markets**, (2) makes a **significant contribution to the customer benefits** of the end product, and (3) is **hard for competitors to imitate**. Most firms have only a handful; a list of 30 'competencies' means you haven't found them.

cards.title: The tree metaphor
cards.body: Prahalad and Hamel's picture: the **roots** are core competencies; the **trunk** is core products (e.g. engines, compressors); the **branches** are business units; the **leaves and fruit** are end products. Judging a company only by its end products is like judging a tree by its leaves.

cards.title: Strategic intent
cards.body: In 1989 Hamel and Prahalad argued winners like Komatsu ('Encircle Caterpillar') and Canon ('Beat Xerox') set an **ambitious, stretching intent** far beyond their resources, then built competencies over years to reach it. Strategy is stretch, not just fit.

cards.title: Bottom of the pyramid (BoP)
cards.body: Billions of the world's poor are an underserved **market**, not just a charity case. To serve them profitably, firms must redesign: **affordability** (small units — sachets), **access** (distribution where people live), **availability**, and **awareness**. Prahalad also argued that serving the poor as customers gives them dignity and choice.

cards.title: BoP in India
cards.body: **Shampoo sachets** let a daily-wage earner buy a single use for a rupee or two. **Aravind Eye Care** performs high volumes of cataract surgery at very low cost with an assembly-line model, cross-subsidising free patients. **HUL's Project Shakti** recruits rural women as distributors. **Jaipur Rugs** links village weavers directly to global buyers.

cards.q: Which of these is the best example of a core competence?
options: Honda's engine and powertrain know-how used across bikes, cars, generators
cards.explain: A core competence is the underlying capability that feeds many products, not a single product.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of Prahalad and Hamel's three tests of a core competence?
cards.explain: The revenue of a product line is irrelevant; the tests are breadth, customer value and inimitability.

cards.q: Selling shampoo in single-use sachets mainly addresses which BoP principle?
cards.explain: Small packs make the purchase affordable for people with daily, irregular cash flow.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Prahalad changed how managers think about two things. First, **what a company really is**: not a portfolio of businesses to buy and sell, but a set of deep capabilities — core competencies — that can grow many businesses. Second, **who the customer can be**: not just the affluent top of the global pyramid, but billions of low-income people who are poorly served and pay a 'poverty penalty' (higher prices for worse goods from moneylenders and middlemen).

Both ideas share a theme: **look beneath the surface.** Beneath products are competencies; beneath 'poverty' is a market that needs innovative business models.

In 'The Core Competence of the Corporation' (HBR, 1990), Prahalad and Hamel contrasted Japanese firms like NEC, which built competencies in semiconductors and digital technology and grew across computers and communications, with Western firms managed as collections of strategic business units (SBUs). The SBU model, they argued, **imprisons competencies**: each unit hoards its talent, and no one invests in capabilities that span units.

Managerial implications:
points: Identify the 5–15 competencies that matter, using the three tests.
Invest in **core products** (components embodying the competence) — even selling them to rivals to gain scale and learning.
Treat key engineers and experts as **corporate resources**, not unit property.
Beware outsourcing activities that are actually competencies.
Use competencies to enter new markets (Honda: motorbikes → cars → lawnmowers → generators → jets).

notes.p: **TCS / Infosys**: the competence is not 'IT services' but large-scale **global delivery** — recruiting and training huge numbers of engineers, managing distributed projects and process quality. It let them move from coding to consulting, BPO, cloud and AI services. **Titan**: precision manufacturing and trusted retail, carried from watches to jewellery (Tanishq) and eyewear. **Asian Paints**: demand forecasting and distribution, which it has carried into home décor. **Bajaj Finance**: fast, data-driven credit decisions at the point of sale, applied across many loan types.

notes.h: Bottom of the pyramid: framework and worked example
notes.p:
*The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid* (2004) argued that serving the poor requires **innovation**, not just cheaper versions of rich-country products. Principles include price-performance at a radically lower price, scale, hybrid technologies, de-skilled work, and education of customers.

**Worked example (illustrative numbers):** A detergent maker sells a 1 kg pack at ₹100 with a ₹15 margin. Rural households can't spare ₹100 at once. It launches a ₹10 sachet (about 80 g) with a ₹1 margin per pack — so per kg the margin is ₹1 × (1,000 ÷ 80) = **₹12.50**, below ₹15 because packaging costs more. But if the sachet reaches 30 crore extra purchases a year, profit = 30 crore × ₹1 = **₹30 crore** from customers who previously bought nothing. The trade-off is lower margin per unit, much bigger volume, and a heavy distribution challenge — which is why HUL built Project Shakti and why the BoP game is won in **distribution**, not just product.

Prahalad's examples included Aravind Eye Care, Jaipur Rugs, ICICI's early micro-finance work, Casas Bahia's credit-based retail in Brazil and Cemex's Patrimonio Hoy home-building savings scheme in Mexico.

Aneel Karnani's 2007 paper 'The Mirage of Marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid' argued the BoP market is much smaller in money terms than claimed, margins are thin, and the real way to help the poor is to **raise their incomes** (treat them as producers, employ them) rather than sell them more products. Sachets also raise **plastic waste** concerns. Micro-finance — once a BoP poster child — saw a crisis in Andhra Pradesh in 2010 over over-lending and harsh recovery. On core competence: the concept is hard to pin down in practice; managers often label anything they do well as a 'core competence'.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Strategy exams ask for the three tests and the tree metaphor; contrast competence-based views with Porter's positioning view (inside-out vs outside-in). Marketing and rural-management roles (FMCG, agri, fintech) use BoP thinking daily — affordability, access, credit, trust. In interviews, 'How would you sell X to rural India?' is a BoP question: talk about pack size, price point, distribution and awareness.

points: Prahalad (1941–2010), Michigan; Indian-born.
**Core competence** (HBR 1990, with Gary Hamel): collective learning that feeds many products.
Three tests: **access to many markets, customer benefit, hard to imitate**.
Tree: competencies (roots) → core products (trunk) → business units → end products.
**Strategic intent** (1989): stretch goals like Komatsu's 'Encircle Caterpillar'.
**BoP** (2004): poor as customers; affordability, access, availability, awareness; poverty penalty.
Indian cases: sachets, Aravind, Project Shakti, Jaipur Rugs.
Critique: Karnani's 'mirage'; waste; micro-finance crisis; competence vagueness.

chapters.title: Henry Mintzberg: what managers really do and emergent strategy

cards.title: The great sceptic
cards.body: Henry Mintzberg (born 1939), a professor at McGill University in Montreal, built a career puncturing management myths — about what managers do, how strategy forms, and even whether MBAs make good managers (*Managers Not MBAs*, 2004). He relies on close observation of real managers rather than theory.

cards.title: Folklore vs fact
cards.body: Mintzberg shadowed chief executives for his 1973 book *The Nature of Managerial Work*. Folklore: managers are reflective, systematic planners. Fact: their work is **brief, varied and fragmented** — about half their activities lasted under nine minutes — and they strongly prefer **verbal**, current information over formal reports.

cards.title: Ten managerial roles
cards.body: Three groups. **Interpersonal**: figurehead, leader, liaison. **Informational**: monitor, disseminator, spokesperson. **Decisional**: entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator. A CEO, a branch manager and a startup founder play all ten in different mixes.

cards.title: Deliberate vs emergent strategy
