cards.body: **Intended** strategy is what you plan. Some becomes **deliberate** (realised as planned); some is **unrealised**. Meanwhile **emergent** strategy forms from patterns in actions nobody planned. **Realised strategy** = deliberate + emergent. Real strategies are almost always a mix.

cards.title: The Five Ps of strategy
cards.body: Mintzberg (1987): strategy can be a **Plan** (intended course), a **Ploy** (manoeuvre to outwit a rival), a **Pattern** (consistency in behaviour over time), a **Position** (place in the market) and a **Perspective** (the firm's way of seeing the world). Most textbooks only teach the first.

cards.title: Honda in America
cards.body: A famous BCG report credited Honda's US motorcycle success to planned scale and low cost. Richard Pascale later interviewed the Honda team: they came to sell **big bikes**, which leaked oil and failed. Staff rode small **Supercubs** around LA, people asked where to buy them, and Honda pivoted. Mintzberg uses this as a model of **emergent** strategy.

cards.title: Crafting strategy
cards.body: In 'Crafting Strategy' (HBR, 1987) Mintzberg compared strategists to a **potter at the wheel**: thinking and acting interleave, ideas come from the clay. In *The Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning* (1994) he argued formal planning can't produce strategy — it can only **programme** strategies already formed.

cards.q: According to Mintzberg, realised strategy is:
cards.explain: Realised = the deliberate part of the intended strategy + emergent patterns that formed along the way.

cards.q: Negotiating a labour contract and handling a factory strike fall under which group of Mintzberg's roles?
cards.explain: Negotiator and disturbance handler are both decisional roles.

cards.q: Zomato began as a restaurant-menu listing site and evolved into food delivery as patterns emerged. This best illustrates:
cards.explain: The delivery strategy emerged from market learning rather than an original master plan.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p: Textbooks describe managers as calm planners who Plan, Organise, Coordinate and Control (the classic list from Henri Fayol). Mintzberg went and watched real managers. He found they are interrupted constantly, juggle dozens of short encounters, prefer phone calls and corridor chats to reports, and make strategy partly by **learning as they go**. His message: stop pretending management is a science of planning; it is a **practice** that blends art (vision), craft (experience) and science (analysis).

In *The Nature of Managerial Work* (1973) and the HBR article 'The Manager's Job: Folklore and Fact' (1975), Mintzberg reported that chief executives worked at an unrelenting pace, that about half of their activities lasted less than nine minutes, and that only a small share lasted more than an hour. He grouped their work into ten roles:
points: **Interpersonal**: figurehead (ceremonial duties), leader (motivating, hiring), liaison (network outside the unit).
**Informational**: monitor (scan for information), disseminator (pass it inside), spokesperson (pass it outside).
**Decisional**: entrepreneur (start change), disturbance handler (crises), resource allocator (who gets what), negotiator.
Implication: managers are the **nerve centre** of information; their advantage is current, informal knowledge — which they must deliberately share.

notes.p:
With James Waters (1985), Mintzberg set out the model: **intended** strategy splits into **deliberate** (realised) and **unrealised**; **emergent** strategy arises from a pattern of actions; together deliberate + emergent = **realised**. Purely deliberate strategy requires perfect foresight and full control; purely emergent strategy means no intentions at all. Both are rare.

The **Honda case** became the centre of a famous debate. The Boston Consulting Group's 1975 report for the British government read Honda's US success as planned experience-curve strategy. Richard Pascale's 1984 interviews with the Honda executives revealed a story of mistakes, luck and fast learning. Mintzberg sided with learning; Michael Goold (a BCG author) and others defended analysis. The modern consensus: you need both.

**Zomato** started in 2008 as Foodiebay, a site listing restaurant menus; it became a discovery and reviews platform, then moved into food delivery around 2015 and later into quick commerce with Blinkit — an emergent path shaped by what customers used. **Infosys's** global delivery model emerged partly from necessity: with limited capital and Indian import restrictions in the 1980s, working offshore and sending staff onsite became the pattern before it was a formal strategy. **Globally**, Netflix moved from DVD rentals to streaming to original content — each step deliberate in execution, but discovered through experiments. **Slack** emerged from a failed online game's internal chat tool.

notes.h: Worked example: reading your own realised strategy
notes.p: Imagine a mid-sized Indian SaaS company whose 3-year plan (intended strategy) said: 70% of revenue from large enterprises, 30% from SMEs, India only. Three years later actual revenue is ₹120 crore: ₹48 crore enterprise (40%), ₹72 crore SME (60%), and ₹30 crore of the total from Southeast Asia, which nobody planned.
points: Deliberate part: enterprise sales happened but at 40% not 70%.
Unrealised: the enterprise-led dominance.
Emergent: SME self-serve growth and Southeast Asian demand (₹30 crore = 25% of revenue).
Mintzberg's advice: don't punish the deviation — **study the emergent pattern**, and if it is working, make it deliberate (fund SME product, build an ASEAN team).

notes.p: Critics such as Igor Ansoff argued that 'emergence' can excuse a lack of strategic thinking — someone still has to decide which emergent patterns to back with capital. His observational studies used small samples (five CEOs in the original study), so generalisation is limited. And his attacks on MBAs are partly self-serving rhetoric; he responded by co-creating the International Masters in Practising Management (IMPM) — which included a module run with the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore — to teach experienced managers through reflection.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Exams love the ten roles (classify a given activity) and the deliberate/emergent diagram. In interviews, 'Tell me about a time a plan didn't work out' is your chance to show emergent learning. In real jobs, keep a monthly note of what you *actually* spent time on vs what you intended — your realised strategy.

points: Mintzberg (McGill): management is art + craft + science, a **practice**.
*The Nature of Managerial Work* (1973): work is brief, varied, fragmented, verbal.
**Ten roles**: interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson), decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).
Intended → deliberate + unrealised; **realised = deliberate + emergent**.
**Five Ps**: plan, ploy, pattern, position, perspective.
Honda US motorcycles: BCG vs Pascale debate.
*Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning* (1994); *Managers Not MBAs* (2004).
Critique: emergence can excuse drift; small samples.

chapters.title: Peter Senge: learning organisations and systems thinking

cards.title: The learning organisation
cards.body: Peter Senge of MIT, in *The Fifth Discipline* (1990), described the **learning organisation**: one where people continually expand their capacity to create the results they truly desire and **learn how to learn together**. His argument: in a fast-changing world, the only lasting advantage may be the ability to learn faster than competitors.

cards.title: The five disciplines
cards.body: (1) **Personal mastery** — continually clarifying what matters to you and seeing reality clearly. (2) **Mental models** — surfacing hidden assumptions. (3) **Shared vision** — a picture people genuinely commit to. (4) **Team learning** — dialogue, thinking together. (5) **Systems thinking** — the 'fifth discipline' that integrates the rest.

cards.title: Systems thinking basics
cards.body: See **wholes and loops** instead of parts and straight lines. **Reinforcing loops** amplify (word-of-mouth growth, or a run on a bank). **Balancing loops** push toward a goal (a thermostat, a price rising until demand falls). **Delays** between cause and effect make people overreact.

cards.title: Learning disabilities
cards.body: Senge's list includes: **'I am my position'** (people see only their own job), **'the enemy is out there'** (blame outsiders), the **illusion of taking charge**, fixation on events, the **parable of the boiled frog** (missing slow threats), and the **myth of the management team** (smart people hiding disagreement).

cards.title: System archetypes
cards.body: Recurring patterns: **Limits to growth** (growth hits a constraint — push the constraint, not growth). **Shifting the burden** (a quick fix weakens the fundamental solution). **Fixes that fail** (the fix has unintended consequences). **Tragedy of the commons** (shared resource overused).

cards.title: The Beer Game
cards.body: In MIT's beer distribution game (rooted in Jay Forrester's system dynamics), players run retailer, wholesaler, distributor and brewery. A small, one-time rise in consumer demand produces huge swings in orders and inventory upstream — even though nobody does anything 'wrong'. The **structure** (delays, no shared information) causes the behaviour.

cards.title: Single- vs double-loop learning
cards.body: From Chris Argyris and Donald Schön: **single-loop** learning corrects actions within existing assumptions (thermostat adjusts heat). **Double-loop** learning questions the assumptions themselves (should the target be 22°C at all?). Learning organisations practise double-loop learning.

cards.q: Which discipline did Senge call 'the fifth discipline' that integrates the others?
cards.explain: Systems thinking is the fifth discipline that ties the other four together.

cards.q: A company keeps offering deep discounts to hit monthly targets, which trains customers to wait for discounts and weakens the brand. This archetype is:
cards.explain: A quick fix (discounts) relieves the symptom while undermining the fundamental solution (brand value).

cards.q: In the Beer Game, the large swings in upstream orders are mainly caused by:
options: System structure — delays and lack of information
cards.explain: Senge's lesson: structure drives behaviour; the bullwhip comes from delays and limited visibility.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
Most management tools break problems into parts: sales targets for the sales team, cost targets for operations. Peter Senge argues that many organisational problems come from **interactions** between the parts — loops, delays and side-effects that no single department sees. Solving these needs **systems thinking** plus four supporting habits. Together they make a **learning organisation** that adapts faster than its environment changes.

Senge's book *The Fifth Discipline* (1990) drew on Jay Forrester's **system dynamics** work at MIT and on Chris Argyris's research on organisational learning.

points: **Personal mastery**: holding a clear personal vision and an honest view of current reality; the gap between them creates 'creative tension' that drives learning.
**Mental models**: the deep assumptions that shape how we see the world (e.g. 'customers only care about price'). Make them explicit and test them.
**Shared vision**: not a slogan from the top but a picture people genuinely own; it creates commitment rather than mere compliance.
**Team learning**: teams that think together, using **dialogue** (exploring ideas without judging) as well as **discussion** (deciding). Teams can be smarter than their members — or dumber.
**Systems thinking**: seeing patterns of interrelationship, feedback loops and delays; the discipline that integrates the other four.

notes.h: Systems thinking: loops, delays and archetypes
notes.p:
Draw cause-and-effect as **loops**. A **reinforcing loop** grows or collapses exponentially: more users → more reviews → more users. A **balancing loop** seeks a goal: higher inventory → fewer orders → lower inventory. **Delays** make balancing loops oscillate — like adjusting a hotel shower where hot water arrives slowly.

Senge's **archetypes** help diagnose patterns. *Limits to growth*: a startup's sales grow fast until delivery capacity or customer support breaks — pushing sales harder just worsens it; fix the constraint. *Shifting the burden*: managers keep fixing problems themselves, so teams never build capability. *Fixes that fail*: building more flyovers in a congested city can induce more traffic. *Tragedy of the commons*: departments overuse a shared IT team or budget.
The beer game shows the **bullwhip effect** found in real supply chains. Illustrative numbers for a soap brand:
points: Shoppers' weekly demand rises once from 100 to 110 cases (+10%) and stays there.
The retailer, seeing stock fall and fearing shortage, orders **120** (to cover demand and rebuild stock).
The distributor sees orders jump 20% and, adding its own safety buffer, orders **140** (+40%).
The factory sees +40% and, with production delays, schedules **170** (+70%).
A few weeks later all the buffers arrive, everyone is over-stocked, and orders crash below 100.

A 10% change at the shelf became a 70% swing at the factory. Fixes: share point-of-sale data upstream, shorten delays, order more frequently in smaller lots. Indian FMCG firms with direct retailer-ordering apps and Asian Paints' frequent-replenishment model attack exactly this.

notes.p: **Global:** Toyota's culture of kaizen and root-cause analysis is a learning organisation in practice; Pixar's 'Braintrust' candid-feedback sessions are team learning; Amazon's written six-page memos and post-incident reviews surface mental models. **India:** the Tata group's internal knowledge-sharing and innovation forums, and Indian IT firms' huge training campuses (Infosys's Mysuru campus) are attempts at organisational learning at scale. In any company, **blameless post-mortems** and asking 'what structure produced this behaviour?' instead of 'who is to blame?' are Senge in action.

'Learning organisation' became a fashionable label that is hard to measure: what exactly counts as learning, and how do you know you have it? Critics say Senge's vision is idealistic, under-weights power, politics and incentives, and is hard to implement in hierarchical cultures — including many Indian family firms where challenging the boss's mental model is risky. System-dynamics models can be built to tell almost any story if assumptions aren't tested. Still, the core tools — loops, delays, archetypes — have proved durable.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: OB exams ask you to list the five disciplines and explain one archetype with an example. Consulting and operations interviews may present a 'why do inventories swing?' case — talk bullwhip, delays and information sharing. In real jobs, sketching a quick loop diagram in a meeting often reveals why a 'fix' keeps failing.

points: Senge, *The Fifth Discipline* (1990), MIT; builds on Forrester's system dynamics.
Five disciplines: **personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, systems thinking**.
Systems thinking: **reinforcing** and **balancing** loops; **delays** cause oscillation.
Learning disabilities: 'I am my position', 'the enemy is out there', boiled frog.
Archetypes: limits to growth, shifting the burden, fixes that fail, tragedy of the commons.
Beer game → **bullwhip effect**; structure drives behaviour.
Argyris & Schön: **single- vs double-loop** learning.
Critique: hard to measure, idealistic, ignores power.

chapters.title: Case: Reliance Jio — pricing that rewired an industry

cards.title: The situation in 2016
cards.body: Before Jio, India had around a dozen mobile operators fighting over voice calls. Data was expensive — often around ₹200–250 per GB — and most users rationed it. 4G coverage was patchy. Reliance Industries, a refining and petrochemicals giant, had been building a nationwide **4G-only** network for years, reportedly investing well over ₹1.5 lakh crore before launch.

cards.title: The decision
cards.body: In September 2016 Jio launched with a **'welcome offer'**: free data and free voice for months, then permanently free voice calls and data at a fraction of prevailing prices. It was not a discount — it was a **reset of the price point**, designed to win share before rivals could respond.

cards.title: What happened
cards.body: Jio reportedly crossed 100 million subscribers in under six months — among the fastest customer ramps in telecom history. Data prices per GB fell by over 90% across India within a few years, and Indians became some of the world's heaviest mobile data users. Rivals' revenues and profits collapsed.

cards.title: Industry consolidation
cards.body: Within a few years the market shrank to essentially **three private players** — Jio, Airtel and Vodafone Idea (the latter formed by the 2018 merger of Vodafone India and Idea) — plus state-owned BSNL. Several operators (Telenor India, Tata Docomo, Aircel, Reliance Communications) sold out, merged or shut down.

cards.title: Ecosystem, not just a network
cards.body: Jio added the **JioPhone** (cheap 4G feature phone), apps for music, video and payments, JioMart commerce and JioFiber broadband. In 2020, **Jio Platforms** raised over ₹1.5 lakh crore by selling minority stakes to investors including **Meta (Facebook)** and **Google** — helping Reliance cut its debt.

cards.title: The economics of a price reset
cards.body: Telecom is a **high fixed cost, near-zero marginal cost** business. Once the network is built, an extra GB costs very little. Profit ≈ (Subscribers × ARPU) − mostly fixed costs. So the winning move is to **fill the network fast**; volume matters more than price per unit, until the market consolidates and prices can rise.

cards.title: Lesson for strategists
cards.body: Jio used three levers together: **scale** (a deep-pocketed parent), **a technology discontinuity** (4G-only network, no legacy 2G/3G costs) and **penetration pricing**. Incumbents with legacy networks and debt couldn't match without destroying their own profits — a Christensen-style dilemma plus Porter-style rivalry.

cards.q: Why could Jio afford near-zero marginal prices for data?
options: Telecom has high fixed costs but very low marginal cost per extra GB
cards.explain: Once the network is built, extra usage costs little, so filling capacity quickly maximises long-run profit.

cards.q: Which outcome followed Jio's entry?
options: Voice calls became more expensive than data
Consolidation to three main private operators
cards.explain: Many operators exited or merged, leaving Jio, Airtel and Vodafone Idea plus BSNL.

cards.q: Jio's strategy is best described as:
cards.explain: Very low entry prices to build scale fast, then layering services on top.

notes.p:
By 2015 India was a crowded mobile market: about a dozen operators, intense price wars on **voice**, low revenue per user, and heavy debts from spectrum auctions. Mobile **data** was a premium product — roughly ₹200–250 per GB was common — and most users were on 2G or patchy 3G. Smartphones were spreading fast, but many people used Wi-Fi or rationed data packs.

Reliance Industries, led by Mukesh Ambani, had bought broadband-wireless spectrum in 2010 through Infotel (later Reliance Jio Infocomm) and spent the following years building a **4G-only, all-IP network** across the country, plus fibre backbone and towers. Reports put the investment before launch at well over ₹1.5 lakh crore. Critics doubted it would ever pay back.
Jio's commercial launch in September 2016 broke every industry convention:
points: **Free** voice and data during a welcome offer that ran for several months.
After that, **voice free for life** (with a temporary interconnect charge episode later) and data priced at a small fraction of rivals' rates.
**Aggressive distribution**: instant e-KYC using Aadhaar let a SIM be activated in minutes rather than days.
**Device strategy**: the JioPhone, an ultra-cheap 4G feature phone, brought feature-phone users onto 4G.
**Ecosystem**: free apps for music, movies, TV and payments to make data valuable.

notes.p:
Subscribers surged — Jio reported crossing 100 million in under six months — and over the following years it became India's largest operator with well over 40 crore subscribers. India's average data use per smartphone user rose from around a gigabyte a month to roughly 20 GB or more. This cheap data underpinned UPI's spread, short-video apps, online education during COVID and India's startup boom.

Incumbents were hit hard. Airtel's profits shrank, Vodafone and Idea merged in 2018 and still struggled with heavy debts and government dues, and several smaller players exited. In 2020, during the pandemic, Jio Platforms sold minority stakes to Meta, Google and a string of investors for over ₹1.5 lakh crore. Once the market had consolidated, the operators raised tariffs several times (notable rounds in 2019, 2021 and 2024), lifting **ARPU**.

notes.h: Worked example: why filling the network wins
notes.p: Illustrative numbers. Suppose an operator's network costs ₹30,000 crore a year to run (depreciation, spectrum, staff, towers) almost regardless of traffic, and the cost of each extra subscriber is small, say ₹20 a month.
points: **Strategy A (premium)**: 10 crore subscribers × ₹250 ARPU/month × 12 = ₹30,000 crore revenue. Variable cost = 10 crore × ₹20 × 12 = ₹2,400 crore. Profit = 30,000 − 30,000 − 2,400 = **−₹2,400 crore**.
**Strategy B (penetration)**: 30 crore × ₹150 × 12 = ₹54,000 crore revenue. Variable cost = 30 crore × ₹20 × 12 = ₹7,200 crore. Profit = 54,000 − 30,000 − 7,200 = **+₹16,800 crore**.
Lower price, three times the users, and the fixed cost is spread far wider. The risk: you burn cash until scale arrives, which only a deep-pocketed parent can fund.
**Cost structure decides strategy**: in high-fixed, low-marginal-cost businesses, scale and utilisation win.
**Technology discontinuities** let entrants leapfrog: no legacy 2G/3G networks to maintain.
**Incumbent's dilemma**: matching Jio's prices would have cannibalised rivals' existing revenue and blown their debt covenants.
**Ecosystems lock in**: content, payments and commerce raise switching costs.
**Consolidation follows price wars**, after which prices rise — a Five Forces shift from many rivals to an oligopoly.
**Regulation matters**: interconnect charges, spectrum pricing and Aadhaar-based e-KYC all shaped the outcome.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** It is October 2016. You are CEO of an incumbent operator with a large 2G/3G base, ₹80,000 crore of debt and profitable voice revenue. Jio is giving everything away free. Do you (a) match prices immediately and accept losses, (b) defend only your high-value customers with bundled plans, (c) merge with a rival to gain scale, or (d) sell your business? Consider cash runway, network quality, brand loyalty and what the market will look like in five years. Airtel chose a mix of (b) and fierce investment in its network; Vodafone and Idea chose (c).

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Consulting interviews use Jio for pricing, market entry and competitive-response cases. Strategy exams pair it with Porter's Five Forces (rivalry → consolidation) and Christensen (low-end/new-market disruption). Telecom, fintech and media jobs still live in the world Jio created: cheap data, mass-market digital users and ARPU as the key metric.

points: 2016 launch: free welcome offer, free voice, very cheap data; 4G-only network.
Reported 100 million users in under six months; data prices fell by over 90%.
Economics: high fixed, low marginal cost → **penetration pricing** to fill capacity.
Industry consolidated to Jio, Airtel, Vodafone Idea (+ BSNL).
Ecosystem: JioPhone, apps, JioMart, JioFiber; 2020 Jio Platforms stake sales to Meta, Google and others.
Tariff hikes after consolidation raised ARPU.
Key frameworks: Five Forces, disruption, ecosystem lock-in.

chapters.title: Case: Amul — a cooperative that built a brand and a nation's milk

cards.title: The situation in 1946
cards.body: Dairy farmers in Kaira (Kheda) district, Gujarat, sold milk through middlemen and a private dairy that supplied Bombay. Prices were set against them; milk, being perishable, gave farmers no bargaining power. Inspired by **Sardar Patel** and led by **Tribhuvandas Patel**, farmers formed the **Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union** at Anand in 1946.

cards.title: Kurien and the Anand pattern
cards.body: **Verghese Kurien**, a young engineer posted to Anand, stayed to build the union. The **Anand pattern**: a three-tier cooperative — **village society** (collects milk, pays farmers), **district union** (processes), **state federation** (markets). Farmers own every tier, and professionals run operations.

cards.title: Technology and brand
cards.body: Amul's team, notably H.M. Dalaya, helped develop a way to make milk powder from **buffalo milk**, which most of Gujarat's farmers had — a technical breakthrough. The **Amul** brand ('amulya', priceless) came in 1955. The **Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF)**, formed in 1973, markets all products under it.

cards.title: Operation Flood
cards.body: Launched in 1970 by the **National Dairy Development Board** (NDDB, chaired by Kurien), Operation Flood replicated the Anand pattern across India in three phases, partly funded by selling donated European dairy commodities. It linked rural milksheds to city markets. India later became the **world's largest milk producer** — the 'White Revolution'.

cards.title: The Amul girl
cards.body: Since 1966 the polka-dotted **Amul girl**, created by the agency daCunha, has commented wittily on current events in hoardings and ads. Topical, cheap to produce and loved for decades, it is a lesson in **consistent brand-building** on a modest budget.

cards.title: Where the consumer's rupee goes
cards.body: Amul's model aims to pass a **high share of the consumer price back to farmers** — commonly cited as around 70–80%. Illustrative: if consumers pay ₹66 per litre and the farmer receives ₹52, the farmer share is 52 ÷ 66 ≈ **79%**. In many private chains, middlemen capture far more.

cards.title: Why it matters to managers
cards.body: Amul shows that **ownership structure** is a strategy choice. A cooperative can win on trust, supply assurance and low prices — but must still hire professional managers, build brands and invest in technology. 'Taste of India' is backed by a supply chain of millions of small farmers.

cards.q: In the Anand pattern, which tier markets products under the Amul brand?
cards.explain: GCMMF, the state-level federation, handles marketing for all member district unions.

cards.q: Operation Flood was launched in 1970 by:
cards.explain: The National Dairy Development Board, chaired by Verghese Kurien, ran Operation Flood.

cards.q: Consumers pay ₹60 per litre and farmers receive ₹48. What is the farmer's share?

notes.p:
In 1940s Gujarat, Kaira district's dairy farmers — mostly small holders with a few buffaloes — had no power. A private dairy with a contract to supply Bombay's milk scheme and a network of middlemen dictated prices. Milk spoils within hours, so a farmer cannot hold out for a better offer. On the advice of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, and with local leader Tribhuvandas Patel, farmers went on a 'milk strike' and in 1946 registered the **Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union**.

Verghese Kurien, a government-posted dairy engineer, arrived in Anand in 1949, intending to leave. He stayed for life, becoming the professional architect of Indian dairy.

notes.h: Decision: a farmer-owned, professionally run value chain
notes.p: The key choices:
points: **Farmer ownership at every tier**: village cooperative societies collect milk twice daily, test fat content and pay farmers promptly — often daily, which mattered enormously to cash-poor households.
**Professional management**: farmers own; trained managers and scientists run plants, R&D and marketing.
**Technology**: buffalo-milk powder and later baby food and cheese — products that turned seasonal surplus into shelf-stable value.
**One brand**: Amul (from 1955), with GCMMF (1973) marketing for all member unions, avoiding competing brands within the cooperative.
**Pricing for the masses**: keep consumer prices low and farmer share high, with thin margins in between.

notes.p:
The model scaled. Operation Flood (from 1970) took the Anand pattern nationwide through NDDB, building cooperative unions and cold chains and linking rural milksheds to cities. India's milk output rose dramatically, and by the late 1990s India had become the world's largest milk producer — a position it still holds. GCMMF grew into one of India's largest food companies, sourcing from roughly 36 lakh farmer members in Gujarat alone, with an annual turnover in the tens of thousands of crore rupees. Amul expanded into butter, cheese, ice cream, chocolates and more, and in recent years into other states and overseas markets.

The brand became one of India's most trusted, helped by the Amul girl hoardings since 1966 — humorous, topical and remarkably consistent.

notes.h: Worked example: cooperative vs middleman economics
notes.p: Illustrative numbers for one litre of milk sold at ₹60 in a city.
points: **Middleman chain**: farmer paid ₹36; collection agent margin ₹6; private processor margin ₹8; distributor & retailer ₹6; processing & transport ₹4. Farmer share = 36 ÷ 60 = **60%**.
**Cooperative chain**: farmer paid ₹47; processing & transport ₹5; distribution & retail ₹6; cooperative surplus ₹2 (partly returned to farmers as bonus). Farmer share = 47 ÷ 60 ≈ **78%**.
For a farmer supplying 10 litres a day, the difference of ₹11/litre is ₹110 a day — about **₹40,000 a year** (110 × 365 = ₹40,150), a life-changing sum for a small household.
The cooperative can still offer consumers a competitive price because it runs on volume and thin margins rather than maximising profit per litre.
**Ownership is strategy**: aligning the owners with the suppliers created trust and reliable supply.
**Professionals + farmers**: democracy at the base, expertise at the top.
**Technology unlocks markets**: buffalo-milk powder solved a real constraint.
**One strong brand** across a federation avoided internal competition.
**Replicable model**: the Anand pattern scaled through NDDB — a platform, not a one-off.
**Shared value before the phrase existed**: social impact and commercial success reinforced each other.
**Risks**: political interference in cooperatives, slower decision-making, and tension between farmer prices and consumer prices.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** You are MD of GCMMF today. Private dairies and D2C brands are attacking premium segments (A2 milk, protein products, organic), while quick-commerce apps demand higher margins. Farmers want higher procurement prices; consumers resist price hikes. Do you (a) launch premium sub-brands under Amul, (b) partner deeply with quick-commerce platforms, (c) expand aggressively to new states where local cooperatives already operate, or (d) focus on farmer productivity (cattle health, feed) to cut costs? How do you protect the cooperative's purpose while competing like a modern FMCG company?

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Marketing interviews: 'Why is Amul's brand so strong?' — talk consistency, trust, value pricing and the Amul girl. Operations: cold chain, procurement and perishables. Strategy and rural management (IRMA was founded at Anand with Kurien's involvement) treat Amul as the classic cooperative case. It pairs well with Porter and Kramer's shared value and Prahalad's bottom of the pyramid.

points: 1946: Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union, Anand; Sardar Patel's advice, Tribhuvandas Patel's leadership.
Verghese Kurien: professional architect; NDDB chairman.
**Anand pattern**: village society → district union → state federation (GCMMF, 1973).
Buffalo-milk powder breakthrough; Amul brand from 1955; Amul girl from 1966.
**Operation Flood** (1970–): White Revolution; India became the world's largest milk producer.
High farmer share of consumer rupee (often cited ~70–80%).
Lessons: ownership as strategy, professional management, one brand, replicable platform.

chapters.title: Case: Tata group — TCS, the Nano and trust-based governance

cards.title: An unusual ownership structure
cards.body: Founded by **Jamsetji Tata** in 1868, the Tata group is controlled by **Tata Sons**, roughly two-thirds of which is owned by **philanthropic Tata Trusts**. So a large part of the group's dividends funds hospitals, research and education. Governance rests on trust, values and long horizons rather than a single family's wealth.

cards.title: TCS: the crown jewel
cards.body: **Tata Consultancy Services** began in 1968 as a division serving group companies. Under F.C. Kohli and later S. Ramadorai it grew through software exports, the Y2K boom and the global delivery model. After its 2004 IPO it became India's largest IT services firm and, for years, the group's largest source of profit.

cards.title: The Nano bet
cards.body: In 2008 Ratan Tata unveiled the **Nano**, promised at about **₹1 lakh** — a safe car for families riding four to a scooter. Engineering triumph: frugal design, target costing. But land protests at **Singur**, West Bengal, forced the plant to move to Sanand, Gujarat, delaying launch to 2009.

cards.title: Why the Nano struggled
cards.body: Marketing it as the **'cheapest car'** stigmatised it — Indian buyers see a car as a status purchase. Early fire incidents hurt trust. Input costs pushed the price up. Sales never reached the planned scale, and production ended around 2018. Ratan Tata later acknowledged the 'cheapest car' positioning was a mistake.

cards.title: Global acquisitions
cards.body: The group went global with **Tetley** (2000), **Corus** steel (2007, among India's biggest overseas deals) and **Jaguar Land Rover** (2008). Corus burdened Tata Steel with high costs in Europe; JLR, bought at the start of the financial crisis, became a major profit driver after a turnaround.

cards.title: Governance tested
cards.body: In 2016 Tata Sons removed chairman **Cyrus Mistry**, triggering a long legal fight; the Supreme Court upheld the removal in 2021. **N. Chandrasekaran** (ex-TCS CEO) became chairman in 2017, simplifying the portfolio and reacquiring **Air India** (completed 2022). Ratan Tata died in October 2024.

cards.title: The lesson
cards.body: Tata's brand value rests on **trust**: paying taxes honestly, refusing bribes, caring for communities (Jamshedpur). That trust lets new ventures — Titan, Tata Capital, Tata Digital — borrow credibility. But trust governance needs clear processes, or it becomes opaque.

cards.q: Who owns roughly two-thirds of Tata Sons?
cards.explain: Philanthropic trusts hold the majority of Tata Sons, so dividends largely flow to charity.

cards.q: The main marketing lesson from the Nano is:
options: Indian buyers want the cheapest possible car
Positioning a status product as 'cheapest' can backfire
Small cars never sell in India
cards.explain: Cars are aspirational; the 'cheapest car' tag stigmatised the Nano.

cards.q: Which Tata acquisition became a major profit driver after a turnaround?
cards.explain: JLR, bought in 2008, became one of the group's biggest earners after its turnaround.

notes.p:
The Tata group is India's oldest and most respected business conglomerate. Jamsetji Tata started in textiles in 1868; his vision gave India its first integrated steel plant (TISCO, now Tata Steel, 1907), hydroelectric power and the Indian Institute of Science. Over a century the group spread into chemicals, hotels (the Taj, 1903), trucks, tea, IT and more.

Its structure is unusual: **Tata Sons**, the holding company, is majority-owned by philanthropic **Tata Trusts**, with the Shapoorji Pallonji group the largest minority holder. Group companies are separately listed. When Ratan Tata became chairman in 1991, the group was a loose federation of semi-independent fiefdoms facing India's newly liberalised market. Three episodes from the following decades teach different lessons: **TCS**, the **Nano**, and **governance**.

points: **TCS (from 1968)**: invest early in software services, train engineers at scale, and later pioneer offshore delivery for global clients. Ratan Tata's era turned it from a division into the group's engine; its 2004 IPO revealed huge value.
**Consolidation (1990s)**: raise Tata Sons' stakes in group companies, retire old satraps, introduce a common Tata brand and code of conduct, and require companies to pay a brand fee.
**Going global (2000–08)**: Tetley, Corus, JLR — bold, debt-funded acquisitions.
**The Nano (2008)**: build a ₹1 lakh car through frugal engineering — fewer parts, rear engine, minimal features, and novel supplier collaboration.
**Succession (2012–17)**: Cyrus Mistry appointed chairman in 2012, removed in 2016; Chandrasekaran appointed in 2017.

notes.p:
**TCS** became the group's crown jewel — India's largest IT services company and, for years, the main source of Tata Sons' dividends. It funded much of the group's ambition.

**The Nano** was an engineering marvel but a commercial disappointment. The Singur agitation forced a costly relocation to Sanand. The 'cheapest car' label clashed with aspirational buying; early fire incidents hurt confidence; costs rose; and used cars and EMIs gave buyers alternatives. Volumes remained far below the planned capacity until production ended around 2018.

**Corus** proved a heavy burden as European steel weakened. **JLR**, by contrast, recovered with new models and strong demand from China and became a major earner, though it remains cyclical.

The **Mistry episode** exposed tension between the Trusts' oversight and the chairman's authority; after courts upheld the removal, Chandrasekaran simplified the portfolio, invested in digital, electronics and semiconductors, and took back Air India.

notes.h: Worked example: target costing the Nano
notes.p: Target costing works backwards from the price customers can pay. Illustrative numbers:
points: Target price to customer: ₹1,00,000. Dealer margin ~₹5,000 and taxes ~₹15,000 leave **₹80,000** ex-factory.
Tata's desired margin ₹4,000 → **target cost ₹76,000** for the whole car.
If engineers estimate ₹72,000 in parts and assembly, profit is ₹8,000 a car — ₹4,000 of buffer above the target margin.

Now steel and other inputs rise 15% on a ₹50,000 material bill: +₹7,500. Cost becomes ₹79,500, so profit per car collapses from ₹8,000 to just **₹500** (₹80,000 − ₹79,500) at ₹1 lakh — one more cost shock and every car sells at a loss.

Options: raise the price (break the promise), cut features (hurt appeal), or absorb losses (needs volume). Tata eventually raised prices, eroding the core 'one-lakh' story. Lesson: an ultra-low price point leaves almost no room for cost shocks.
**Patient, trust-based ownership** lets a group back long bets like TCS — and makes the Tata name a valuable umbrella brand.
**Positioning matters as much as engineering**: the Nano proved frugal innovation possible but mis-read the customer's emotional 'job' (status, safety, pride).
**Acquisitions need timing and integration**: JLR succeeded; Corus showed the cost of paying a high price at a cycle peak.
**Governance must be explicit**: trusteeship and ethics need clear roles between owners, board and CEO.
**Portfolio discipline**: simplifying from many businesses into focused verticals unlocked value.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** It is 2010. Nano sales are far below plan. You are on the Tata Motors board. Do you (a) reposition the Nano as a smart city car for young urban buyers with more features at a higher price, (b) keep it as India's cheapest car and push rural financing, (c) stop production and write off the investment, or (d) use the platform for an electric micro-car? Weigh brand damage, sunk costs (remember they are sunk), Ratan Tata's personal commitment and the factory's alternative uses.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Marketing interviews: the Nano is the go-to example of positioning failure and of frugal innovation. Strategy and corporate governance courses use the Mistry case to discuss board powers, minority shareholders and trusts. M&A modules contrast Corus and JLR. In Tata group interviews, expect questions about values and the trust structure.

points: Founded 1868 by Jamsetji Tata; **Tata Sons ~two-thirds owned by Tata Trusts**.
**TCS** (1968): from internal division to India's largest IT services firm; IPO 2004.
**Nano** (unveiled 2008, ₹1 lakh target): Singur → Sanand; 'cheapest car' positioning failed; ended ~2018.
**Corus** (2007) weighed on Tata Steel; **JLR** (2008) turned around.
**Mistry** removed 2016; SC upheld 2021; **Chandrasekaran** chairman from 2017; Air India back in 2022.
Lessons: trust as brand, positioning beats engineering, governance clarity, target costing risks.

chapters.title: Case: Infosys — the global delivery model and governance

cards.title: The situation in 1981
cards.body: Seven engineers led by **N.R. Narayana Murthy** — including Nandan Nilekani, S. Gopalakrishnan and S.D. Shibulal — founded Infosys in Pune in 1981 with about ₹10,000 of seed capital, famously borrowed from Sudha Murty. India then had import licences, slow phone connections and long waits for computers. Building a software company was very hard.

cards.title: The global delivery model
cards.body: Infosys and peers refined the **Global Delivery Model (GDM)**: split work so a small team works **onsite** with the client (requirements, coordination) while most development happens **offshore** in India at much lower cost. Time-zone differences enabled near round-the-clock work. Rigorous process quality (CMM Level 5) reassured clients.

cards.title: Liberalisation as the turning point
cards.body: The **1991 reforms** removed many barriers: easier imports of hardware, better telecom links, and later software technology parks with satellite connectivity. Infosys listed in India in **1993** and on **NASDAQ in 1999** — reportedly the first India-registered company to list on a US exchange.

cards.title: Governance as a brand
cards.body: Infosys built its reputation on transparency: early adoption of global accounting and disclosure standards, independent directors, and **ESOPs** that shared wealth widely with employees. Murthy's personal frugality reinforced the message. Good governance helped win global clients who were nervous about outsourcing to India.

cards.title: Onsite–offshore blended rate
cards.body: **Blended rate = (onsite share × onsite rate) + (offshore share × offshore rate).** If onsite bills $90/hr and offshore $30/hr, a 30:70 mix gives 0.3 × 90 + 0.7 × 30 = 27 + 21 = **$48/hr** — almost half the all-onsite cost, while giving the vendor healthy margins.

cards.title: Governance crisis 2017
cards.body: **Vishal Sikka**, the first non-founder CEO from outside, pushed into software products and automation. Founders, led by Murthy, publicly questioned severance pay to departing executives and the Panaya acquisition. Sikka resigned in 2017; **Nilekani returned as chairman** and **Salil Parekh** became CEO in 2018.

cards.title: The deeper lesson
cards.body: Infosys shows that **processes and trust** can be a moat in services, but founder influence after handing over control is delicate. Boards must balance founders' moral authority with professional management's right to run the company.

cards.q: Onsite rate $100/hr, offshore $25/hr, mix 20% onsite and 80% offshore. Blended rate?
Which event most enabled Indian IT's rapid growth in the 1990s?
cards.explain: 1991 reforms eased imports, telecom and foreign exchange constraints.

cards.q: Who became Infosys CEO in 2018 after the Sikka-era crisis?
cards.explain: Salil Parekh became CEO; Nilekani returned as non-executive chairman.

notes.p:
In 1981 India's economy was closed and controlled. Importing a computer required licences that could take years; foreign exchange was rationed; a telephone line could take months to get. Seven engineers from Patni Computer Systems — Narayana Murthy, Nandan Nilekani, S. Gopalakrishnan, S.D. Shibulal, K. Dinesh, N.S. Raghavan and Ashok Arora — started Infosys in Pune and soon moved to Bengaluru. The company's early work was sending engineers abroad to work on client sites ('body shopping'), which earned modest margins and gave little control.

The question: how could an Indian company build a global, high-quality, respected software business from India?

points: **Offshore delivery**: shift as much work as possible to Indian development centres, with a thin onsite layer — the core of the **Global Delivery Model**.
**Process and quality**: invest in methodologies and certifications (ISO, SEI-CMM Level 5) so clients could trust remote teams.
**Talent factory**: hire graduates at scale and train them; the Mysuru campus became one of the world's largest corporate training centres.
**Governance and transparency**: publish financials under global standards, appoint independent directors, separate roles; share wealth through ESOPs.
**Capital markets**: list in India (1993) and on NASDAQ (1999) to gain capital, visibility and a currency for global credibility.

notes.p:
After liberalisation in 1991, telecom and import barriers fell, and the Y2K problem and the dot-com boom created a surge of demand for programmers. Infosys grew rapidly through the 1990s and 2000s, becoming one of India's largest companies and a symbol of the 'new India'. Its ESOPs created thousands of employee millionaires, which was new in Indian business.

The founders rotated through CEO roles until 2014, when **Vishal Sikka**, an SAP veteran, became the first outsider CEO. He pushed automation, AI and products. Founders, chiefly Murthy, publicly criticised governance decisions, including large severance packages and the 2015 acquisition of Israeli firm Panaya. Sikka resigned in August 2017, blaming the attacks. Nilekani returned as chairman and Salil Parekh took over as CEO in 2018, focusing on digital, cloud and later AI services. Like all IT majors, Infosys now faces a new inflection point as generative AI changes how software is built and billed.
Illustrative 20-person project for a US bank, billed hourly, 2,000 hours per person per year.
points: **All onsite**: 20 people × 2,000 hrs × $90 = **$3.6 million** a year to the client.
**GDM 25:75**: 5 onsite × 2,000 × $90 = $0.9m; 15 offshore × 2,000 × $30 = $0.9m. Total **$1.8 million** — the client saves 50%.

**Vendor margin**: suppose onsite cost is $70/hr and offshore cost is $15/hr. Cost = 5 × 2,000 × 70 + 15 × 2,000 × 15 = $0.7m + $0.45m = $1.15m. Profit = 1.8 − 1.15 = **$0.65m**, a margin of about **36%**.
Win-win: lower bills for clients, high margins for the vendor — as long as wage gaps and productivity hold. Rising Indian wages, visa limits and automation all squeeze this model.
**Constraints breed innovation**: lack of capital and connectivity pushed Infosys toward a scalable, asset-light delivery model.
**Trust is the product** in services: processes, certifications and transparent governance substituted for brand recognition.
**Share the wealth**: ESOPs aligned employees with owners and attracted talent.
**Policy shapes industries**: 1991 reforms and software technology parks were essential tailwinds.
**Founder transitions are hard**: moral authority without formal power can destabilise a professional CEO.
**Models expire**: labour arbitrage is not a permanent moat; value must move up (consulting, platforms, AI).

notes.p: **Discussion question:** You are Infosys's CEO in 2026. Clients expect generative AI to cut the effort on many projects by a large share, and they want lower prices. If you bill by effort (people × hours), AI reduces your revenue. Do you (a) shift to outcome-based or fixed-price contracts and keep the productivity gains, (b) pass savings to clients to win market share, (c) build your own AI platforms and IP, or (d) retrain large parts of the workforce for new roles? How do you manage employees, margins and investor expectations during the transition?

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: For IT-services, consulting and operations roles, you should be able to explain GDM, blended rates, utilisation and pyramid structure. Corporate governance courses use the 2017 episode to discuss founders, boards and independent directors. Interviewers at IT firms often ask how AI changes the services business model.

points: Founded 1981 in Pune by Murthy and six co-founders with ~₹10,000.
**Global Delivery Model**: thin onsite, large offshore; process quality (CMM Level 5).
**Blended rate** = Σ(share × rate); onsite/offshore arbitrage drove margins.
1991 liberalisation + Y2K + dot-com boom = growth.
Listed in India 1993, NASDAQ 1999; ESOPs created widespread employee wealth.
Governance as brand; 2017 Sikka–founders clash; Nilekani back, Salil Parekh CEO 2018.
Today: AI threatens effort-based billing.

chapters.title: Case: Zomato, Swiggy and quick commerce — unit economics

cards.title: The situation
cards.body: **Zomato** began in 2008 as Foodiebay, a site listing restaurant menus; **Swiggy** launched in 2014 as a delivery-first platform in Bengaluru. Food delivery took off around 2015–16, with dozens of funded startups, deep discounts and heavy cash burn. The question every investor asked: **can delivering a ₹400 order ever make money?**

cards.title: Consolidation into a duopoly
cards.body: Most rivals died or sold. Zomato bought **Uber Eats India** in 2020; Amazon and Ola exited or scaled back food. By the early 2020s, Zomato and Swiggy shared nearly all of the market. Zomato listed in 2021; Swiggy in late 2024. Zomato's parent was renamed **Eternal** in 2025.

cards.title: Contribution per order
cards.body:
**Contribution = Revenue per order − Variable costs per order.**
Revenue = restaurant commission + customer fees + ads. Variable costs = rider pay + discounts + payment gateway + support. Fixed costs (tech, head office, brand) are covered only if contribution × orders exceeds them.

cards.title: Illustrative food order
cards.body: Order value ₹450. Commission 20% = ₹90; customer delivery & platform fees ₹25; ads ₹10 → revenue **₹125**. Rider cost ₹75; discounts ₹10; payment gateway ₹9; support & other ₹6 → costs **₹100**. Contribution **₹25** ≈ 5.6% of order value. Thin — so scale and order frequency matter enormously.

cards.title: The levers that turned profits
cards.body: Platforms raised **average order values**, introduced small **platform fees** (from 2023), grew **advertising** income from restaurants, cut **discounts**, launched **memberships** (Zomato Gold, Swiggy One) to raise frequency, and improved rider batching. Zomato's food business turned profitable around 2023.

cards.title: Quick commerce: 10-minute delivery
cards.body: **Blinkit** (acquired by Zomato in 2022), **Swiggy Instamart** and **Zepto** deliver groceries in about 10–20 minutes from **dark stores** — small warehouses within a few km of customers. The model's economics depend on **orders per store per day**: dark-store rent and staff are fixed, so throughput is everything.

cards.title: Watch the critics
cards.body: Restaurants complain about high commissions and platforms' private-label kitchens; the CCI has examined these practices. Gig workers' pay and safety are under scrutiny; several states have passed or proposed gig-worker welfare laws. Kirana stores fear quick commerce. Sustainable unit economics must survive these pressures.

cards.q: Using the formula, a platform earns ₹110 revenue per order and spends ₹80 on rider, ₹15 on discounts and ₹8 on payment fees. Contribution per order?
A dark store's fixed costs are ₹9 lakh/month. At 30,000 orders a month, fixed cost per order is:
Which is the strongest lever for quick-commerce profitability?
options: More dark stores regardless of demand
Higher orders per dark store per day
cards.explain: Fixed dark-store costs fall per order as throughput rises.

notes.p:
India's food-delivery market looked impossible on paper. Average order values were low (a few hundred rupees), labour for last-mile delivery was cheap but not free, restaurants had thin margins, and customers were very price-sensitive. Yet smartphones, cheap data after 2016 and UPI created huge demand for convenience. Venture capital poured in: platforms competed with discounts and free delivery, and many lost money on every order.

Zomato, founded by Deepinder Goyal and Pankaj Chaddah, started as a restaurant-discovery site and moved into delivery around 2015. Swiggy, founded by Sriharsha Majety, Nandan Reddy and Rahul Jaimini, was delivery-first with its own rider fleet from day one.

points: **Own the logistics**: build rider fleets rather than relying on restaurants' own staff — control over speed and reliability.
**Win density first**: focus on large cities where order density keeps rider cost per order low.
**Consolidate**: Zomato bought Uber Eats India (2020) in an all-stock deal; Swiggy and Zomato emerged as a duopoly.
**Raise revenue per order**: commissions, platform fees, ads, memberships.
**Expand adjacencies**: Zomato bought Blinkit (2022) for quick commerce; Swiggy built Instamart; both added dining-out and events.
**Go public**: Zomato's 2021 IPO was a landmark for Indian consumer-internet companies; Swiggy followed in 2024.

notes.p: Discount wars cooled after consolidation. By around 2023 Zomato reported profits as its food-delivery business generated positive contribution and adjusted EBITDA, while Blinkit scaled rapidly. Swiggy narrowed losses but was still investing heavily in Instamart at its listing. **Quick commerce** became the new battleground, with Zepto raising large funding rounds and big players such as Flipkart, Amazon, BigBasket and Reliance entering fast delivery. Dark-store counts climbed into the thousands across cities, and quick commerce began to take share from kiranas and e-commerce for everyday items.

Illustrative numbers for one dark store with fixed costs (rent, staff, power, tech) of **₹11 lakh per month**. Each order has average value ₹550 and gross margin plus ad income of 18% = **₹99**. Variable costs per order: rider ₹35, wastage and packaging ₹8, discounts ₹15 = **₹58**. So contribution before store costs = 99 − 58 = **₹41 per order**.
points: **At 1,500 orders/day** (45,000/month): store cost per order = 11,00,000 ÷ 45,000 ≈ **₹24.4**. Profit per order ≈ 41 − 24.4 = **₹16.6**; monthly store profit ≈ ₹7.5 lakh.
**At 700 orders/day** (21,000/month): store cost per order = 11,00,000 ÷ 21,000 ≈ **₹52.4**. Profit per order ≈ 41 − 52.4 = **−₹11.4**; monthly loss ≈ ₹2.4 lakh.
Break-even orders/month = 11,00,000 ÷ 41 ≈ **26,800** (about 900 a day).
Lesson: the same store is profitable or loss-making depending on **throughput**. That is why players fight for dense neighbourhoods and push higher order values.
**Unit economics before scale**: contribution per order must be positive, or growth multiplies losses.
**Density beats coverage**: rider and store costs fall per order only when demand is concentrated.
**Network effects are local**: being big in India doesn't help if you are small in a particular neighbourhood.
**Duopolies form in platform markets** with high fixed costs and two-sided networks — Porter's rivalry eases after consolidation.
**Multiple revenue streams** (commissions, fees, ads, memberships) make thin-margin businesses viable.
**Stakeholders matter**: restaurants, riders, regulators and kiranas can all push back.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** You run a quick-commerce platform. Your rival just cut delivery fees to zero in your top three cities, and your investors want a path to profitability within 18 months. Do you (a) match the free delivery, (b) focus on raising order value through higher-margin categories like electronics and beauty, (c) close your weakest 20% of dark stores, or (d) sell ads and data services to brands to subsidise delivery? Use the dark-store break-even math to argue your answer.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Product, strategy and consulting interviews constantly ask unit-economics questions about delivery apps: 'Estimate contribution per order', 'How would you make quick commerce profitable?', 'Should Zomato enter X?' Be ready to set out revenue streams, variable costs and fixed-cost absorption. Category-management and supply-chain roles in these firms are popular MBA placements.

points: Zomato (2008, as Foodiebay) and Swiggy (2014) → duopoly after Uber Eats India deal (2020).
**Contribution per order** = commission + fees + ads − (rider + discounts + PG + support).
Profit levers: AOV, platform fees, ads, memberships, fewer discounts, batching.
Zomato bought **Blinkit** (2022); Swiggy built **Instamart**; **Zepto** founded 2021.
Dark stores: fixed costs → **throughput** decides profit; break-even = fixed cost ÷ contribution.
Pressures: restaurant commissions, gig-worker welfare, kirana competition.

chapters.title: Case: Asian Paints — distribution and data as a moat

cards.title: The situation in 1942
cards.body: Four friends started Asian Paints in a Mumbai garage in 1942. Foreign brands dominated India's paint market and focused on big cities. Wartime import restrictions created an opening for a local maker. The founders chose to target the **small towns and rural markets** the multinationals ignored.

cards.title: Small packs and dealers
cards.body: Asian Paints sold in **small pack sizes** affordable to ordinary households and built relationships directly with thousands of small dealers. The cheeky mascot **Gattu**, drawn by cartoonist R.K. Laxman, made the brand friendly. Within a couple of decades it was a national leader.

cards.title: Data before it was cool
cards.body: Asian Paints invested in **mainframe computing in the 1970s**, far earlier than most Indian firms, to analyse dealer-level sales and forecast demand. Paint demand is highly seasonal (festivals like Diwali) and spread across thousands of SKUs. Better forecasting meant the right shade in the right town at the right time.

cards.title: The replenishment machine
cards.body: Instead of loading dealers with stock, Asian Paints built a network of regional distribution centres and depots that **restock dealers frequently** — in many towns more than once a day. Dealers hold less inventory, tie up less cash and rarely run out. That makes Asian Paints the dealer's favourite supplier.

cards.title: Tinting: postponement in action
cards.body: Dealer **tinting machines** mix a few base paints with colourants on the spot to produce thousands of shades. This is **postponement**: delay final customisation until the customer orders, cutting inventory while widening choice — a classic supply-chain strategy.

cards.title: New competition
cards.body: Asian Paints held the largest share of India's decorative paints market for decades. In 2024 the Aditya Birla group's **Birla Opus** entered with a planned investment of around ₹10,000 crore, alongside JSW Paints and established rivals like Berger. Dealer incentives and discounts intensified — a test of how durable the distribution moat is.

cards.title: The lesson
cards.body: Asian Paints' moat is not the paint — chemistry can be copied. It is the **system**: forecasting, depots, frequent replenishment, tinting, dealer relationships and painter networks. That's Porter's **fit** and Buffett's **moat** in one Indian case.

cards.q: Tinting machines at dealers are an example of:
cards.explain: Final product differentiation is delayed until the order, reducing inventory while offering many shades.

cards.q: A dealer sells ₹10,000 of paint per day. Average inventory falls from ₹3 lakh to ₹60,000. Inventory days fall from:
What is the core of Asian Paints' moat?
options: An integrated distribution and data system dealers rely on
cards.explain: Its advantage lies in forecasting, frequent replenishment and dealer relationships — hard to copy as a system.

notes.p:
Asian Paints was founded in 1942 by Champaklal Choksey, Chimanlal Choksi, Suryakant Dani and Arvind Vakil. India's paint market was then dominated by established, largely foreign-owned companies that served large cities and industrial customers. Wartime and post-war import restrictions made imported paint scarce.

Paint is a tricky product: thousands of shades and pack sizes, bulky and heavy, highly seasonal (most homes are painted before Diwali and weddings), and bought through small neighbourhood dealers who recommend brands to customers and painters. Whoever controls availability at the dealer wins.

points: **Go where others aren't**: focus on small towns and rural India with affordable small packs.
**Direct dealer relationships**: sell to dealers directly rather than through large wholesalers, building loyalty and data.
**Invest in data early**: computerise in the 1970s to analyse sales by dealer, shade and season; build forecasting capability.
**Frequent replenishment**: regional distribution centres and depots that resupply dealers often, reducing dealer inventory and stock-outs.
**Tinting systems**: equip dealers with machines to mix shades on demand.
**Move closer to the consumer**: colour consultancy, painting services, home décor and 'Beautiful Homes' stores in later years.

notes.p:
Asian Paints became India's largest paint company by the late 1960s and held a dominant share of the decorative paints market for decades — often estimated at over half. It expanded into many countries in Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and diversified into kitchens, bath fittings and décor. Its return on capital stayed high for years, and it became one of India's most valuable consumer companies.

In the 2020s, the moat was tested. Grasim's **Birla Opus** launched in 2024 with large capacity and aggressive dealer terms, JSW Paints scaled up, and existing rivals pushed harder. Asian Paints' growth slowed and margins came under pressure, showing that even strong moats need constant reinvestment.

notes.h: Worked example: what frequent replenishment is worth
notes.p: Illustrative dealer selling ₹36 lakh of paint a year at cost — about **₹10,000 per day** (using 360 days).
points: **Monthly delivery**: the dealer orders a month's stock (₹3 lakh), so average cycle stock is ₹1.5 lakh; add ₹1.5 lakh of safety stock to avoid stock-outs → average inventory **₹3 lakh** = 30 days.
**Delivery every two days**: order ₹20,000 each time, average cycle stock ₹10,000; safety stock can fall to ₹50,000 because a reorder arrives fast → average inventory **₹60,000** = 6 days.
Cash freed per dealer: 3,00,000 − 60,000 = **₹2.4 lakh**. At 18% cost of credit, that saves the dealer about **₹43,200 a year** (2,40,000 × 0.18).
Across, say, 50,000 dealers, ₹2.4 lakh × 50,000 = **₹1,200 crore** of working capital released in the channel.
Result: dealers love the brand that frees their cash and never stocks out, and they push it to customers and painters.
**Distribution can be the product** in a fragmented retail market.
**Data and forecasting** were a competitive weapon decades before 'big data'.
**Postponement** (tinting) delivers variety without inventory explosion.
**Win the channel's economics**: make dealers more profitable and they become your sales force.
**Fit**: forecasting, depots, tinting and dealer relationships reinforce each other — hard to copy piece by piece.
**Moats erode**: a deep-pocketed entrant willing to accept losses can buy dealer loyalty for a while; incumbents must keep innovating.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** It is 2025. A well-funded rival is offering dealers higher margins and credit, and some of your dealers are stocking both brands. Do you (a) match dealer margins and accept lower profit, (b) double down on service — faster replenishment, painter loyalty programmes and tech tools for dealers, (c) cut consumer prices to protect share, or (d) move up into premium services (painting, décor, waterproofing) where the rival is weaker? Which choice uses your moat rather than fighting on the rival's terms?

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Operations and supply-chain courses use Asian Paints for forecasting, postponement and the bullwhip effect. Sales and distribution roles at FMCG and paints firms (popular summer internships) require knowing dealer economics, ROI per dealer and channel incentives. In strategy interviews, it is the classic Indian example of a distribution moat.

points: Founded 1942 in Mumbai by four friends; targeted small towns and rural India.
Small packs, direct dealer relationships, Gattu mascot.
Early **mainframe computing** (1970s) for forecasting.
**Frequent replenishment** from depots → low dealer inventory, few stock-outs.
**Tinting** = postponement: thousands of shades from a few bases.
Market leader in decorative paints for decades; challenged by **Birla Opus** (2024) and others.
Moat = system fit, not chemistry.

chapters.title: Case: HUL Project Shakti and rural marketing

cards.title: The situation around 2000
cards.body: Hindustan Unilever (HUL, then HLL) already reached many Indian villages, but hundreds of thousands of small villages were too tiny, scattered and poorly connected for vans and distributors to serve profitably. Meanwhile local rivals like **Nirma** had shown how fiercely price-sensitive rural consumers could be won.

cards.title: The decision: Project Shakti
cards.body: Launched in 2001 in Andhra Pradesh, **Project Shakti** recruited rural women — often members of **self-help groups** — as micro-entrepreneurs ('Shakti Ammas'). They buy HUL products from a distributor and sell door-to-door and to small shops in their own and nearby villages, earning a margin.

cards.title: Why it works
cards.body: The Shakti entrepreneur solves the **last-mile cost problem**: she lives in the village, has no van or rent, and knows every household. She also builds **trust** and educates customers about hygiene and new products. For HUL it's a low-cost, scalable channel; for her it's income and status.

cards.title: The 4 As of rural marketing
cards.body: Jagdish Sheth and Rajendra Sisodia's **4 As** fit rural India well: **Availability** (reach the village), **Affordability** (small packs, low price points), **Acceptability** (products suited to local needs) and **Awareness** (haats, melas, wall paintings, local media, influencers).

cards.title: The sachet revolution
cards.body: Rural buying runs on **daily cash flows**. Sachets of shampoo and other products — pioneered in India by smaller southern firms such as Velvette and CavinKare's Chik, then scaled by HUL and others — made branded goods affordable one use at a time. Price points like ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10 became sacred.

cards.title: Nirma vs Surf
cards.body: In the 1970s–80s, Karsanbhai Patel's **Nirma** detergent sold at a fraction of Surf's price and grew rapidly in small towns and villages. HUL responded with a cheaper brand, **Wheel**, built a separate low-cost business system for it, and kept Surf for the premium end — a classic case of fighting low-end disruption with a separate unit.

cards.title: Rural is not 'urban minus money'
cards.body: Rural consumers are value-seekers, not just low spenders. Income is seasonal (harvests), word-of-mouth matters, and retailers extend credit. Products and communication must be designed for these realities — not shrunk-down city versions.

cards.q: Project Shakti mainly addresses which of the 4 As?
cards.explain: It solves the cost of reaching small villages — availability — while also helping awareness.

cards.q: HUL's response to Nirma was primarily to:
options: Launch a separate low-priced brand, Wheel, with its own cost structure
cards.explain: Wheel let HUL compete at the low end without destroying Surf's premium margins.

cards.q: A Shakti entrepreneur sells ₹18,000 a month at an average margin of 12%. Her monthly earnings are:

notes.p:
Around two-thirds of Indians live in rural areas, spread across more than six lakh villages. In 2000, HUL's distribution reached the larger villages through wholesalers and stockists, but many smaller villages — a few hundred households each, linked by poor roads — were uneconomic to serve directly. A van-based route needs enough sales per stop to cover fuel, salary and the vehicle.

At the same time, competitors had shown the rural opportunity. **Nirma** had grabbed a huge share of detergents with very low prices, and sachet pioneers had proved rural households would buy brands in tiny units. HUL needed a way to reach the next layer of villages profitably — and ideally to grow the market, not just take share.
HUL designed **Project Shakti**, launched in 2001 in Andhra Pradesh's Nalgonda district and scaled across states:
points: Recruit women from **self-help groups** (SHGs) as 'Shakti Ammas' — direct-to-home distributors.
Provide training in selling, accounts and product knowledge; initial stock was often funded through SHG micro-loans.
The entrepreneur buys from an HUL rural distributor and sells within her village and nearby ones; margins of roughly 10% are commonly reported.
Later, **'Shaktimaan'** — often male family members on bicycles — extended reach to surrounding villages.
Use technology over time: mobile ordering apps for entrepreneurs, digital payments and data on village demand.

notes.p: Shakti grew into a network that HUL has described as including well over a lakh entrepreneurs, reaching a large share of rural India. It became a widely taught case in business schools as an example of **inclusive business** — creating income for rural women while building a profitable channel. Studies and company reports point to higher household incomes and confidence among participants, though the earnings of individual entrepreneurs vary widely and some drop out. The model inspired similar programmes by other FMCG companies, telecom firms and banks (e.g. business correspondents for financial inclusion).

notes.h: Worked example: van route vs Shakti
notes.p: Illustrative numbers.
points: **Van route**: one van with driver and salesman costs ₹2,500 a day and visits 10 small villages, selling ₹2,000 per village = ₹20,000 a day. If HUL's gross margin on these products is 10%, gross profit = ₹2,000 — **less than the ₹2,500 cost**, a daily loss of ₹500.

**Shakti model**: HUL sells to a rural distributor, who supplies 10 Shakti entrepreneurs; each sells ₹18,000 a month at a 12% margin and earns **₹2,160 a month**. HUL's incremental cost is mainly training and the distributor's margin, with no van in the villages.
Village sales = 10 × ₹18,000 = **₹1.8 lakh a month** of new, profitable volume from villages the van couldn't serve.
Lesson: the channel's cost structure, not the product, decided whether these villages were profitable.
**4 As**: availability, affordability, acceptability, awareness — all must be solved together.
**Small unit packs** match daily cash flows; price points matter more than per-gram price.
**Trusted local intermediaries** (Shakti, ASHA workers, kirana owners) beat mass media for new categories.
**Separate business systems** for low-price brands (Wheel vs Surf) avoid cannibalising premium margins.
**Inclusive models** can be good business — Prahalad's bottom-of-the-pyramid logic in action.
**Seasonality**: plan around harvests, festivals and wedding seasons.
**Rural media**: haats, melas, wall paintings, local radio and now short-video apps.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** It is 2026. Rural India has smartphones and UPI, and B2B ordering apps (and some quick-commerce players) promise to supply village kiranas directly. Shakti entrepreneurs' door-to-door model faces new competition. As HUL's rural head, do you (a) turn Shakti entrepreneurs into digital agents who take orders on an app for households and kiranas, (b) shift them toward high-touch categories like beauty and health advice, (c) phase out the programme in well-connected villages, or (d) open Shakti to sell other companies' products (financial services, mobile recharges) to raise their incomes? Consider purpose, cost and the entrepreneurs' livelihoods.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: FMCG marketing and sales roles (HUL, ITC, P&G, Dabur, Marico) are among the most sought-after MBA placements, and rural sales stints are common for management trainees. Interviewers ask 'How would you launch product X in rural India?' — answer with the 4 As, price points, channel economics and local communication. Marketing exams use Shakti and Nirma–Wheel as standard cases.

points: **Project Shakti** (2001, Andhra Pradesh): rural women from SHGs as direct-to-home distributors.
Solves last-mile **availability** at low cost; adds trust and awareness.
Shaktimaan extended reach; tech and apps added later.
**4 As** (Sheth & Sisodia): availability, affordability, acceptability, awareness.
**Sachets** match daily cash flows; key price points ₹1–₹10.
**Nirma vs Surf → Wheel**: separate low-cost business system.
Lesson: channel cost structure decides rural profitability; inclusive business can be good business.

chapters.title: Case: Netflix — pivots, culture and content strategy

cards.title: The situation in 1997
cards.body: Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph founded Netflix in 1997 to rent DVDs by mail. Blockbuster dominated with thousands of stores and earned a lot from **late fees**. Netflix's insight: a **subscription** with no late fees, a big catalogue and a recommendation engine could beat stores for many customers.

cards.title: Pivot 1: DVD subscription
cards.body: By 1999 Netflix offered unlimited DVD rentals for a monthly fee. Around 2000, Netflix reportedly offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for about $50 million — Blockbuster declined. Over the next decade Netflix grew while Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

cards.title: Pivot 2: Streaming
cards.body: In 2007 Netflix launched streaming, cannibalising its own profitable DVD business. In 2011 it tried to split DVDs into a separate service, **Qwikster**, with a steep effective price rise. Customers revolted, Netflix lost subscribers and its stock fell sharply. It dropped Qwikster within weeks — but kept the bet on streaming.

cards.title: Pivot 3: Original content
cards.body: Studios started pulling licensed content as they saw Netflix as a rival. Netflix responded by commissioning **originals**, starting with *House of Cards* (2013), using viewing data to guide bets. Owning content reduced dependence on suppliers — Porter's **supplier power** in action.

cards.title: Going global
cards.body: In January 2016 Netflix launched in about 130 new countries at once. In India it debuted originals like *Sacred Games* (2018) and introduced a cheaper **mobile-only plan** (2019), later cutting prices to compete with local rivals and cheap data-driven viewing habits.

cards.title: Culture: freedom and responsibility
cards.body: Netflix's 2009 'culture deck' became famous: hire high performers, give **freedom with responsibility**, pay top of market, and use the **keeper test** — would a manager fight to keep this person? If not, give them a generous severance. Explained further in *No Rules Rules* (2020) by Hastings and Erin Meyer.

cards.title: Fixed-cost content economics
cards.body: Content is a **fixed cost** spread across subscribers. A $100 million series watched by a base of 250 million subscribers costs $0.40 per subscriber; for a service with 25 million it costs $4. Scale lets the biggest platform spend more on content and still charge less per user — a powerful flywheel.

cards.q: Netflix's 2007 move into streaming while its DVD business was profitable is an example of:
options: Self-cannibalisation to lead the next technology
cards.explain: Netflix chose to disrupt itself rather than wait for others to do it.

cards.q: Why did Netflix shift heavily into original content after around 2013?
options: Studios were pulling licences as they launched rival services, raising supplier power
cards.explain: Owning content reduced dependence on studios that were becoming competitors.

cards.q: A $60 million film is watched across a 200 million subscriber base. Cost per subscriber?

notes.p:
In the late 1990s, renting a film meant driving to a video store. Blockbuster was the giant, with thousands of stores and a business model that earned meaningful revenue from **late fees** — a source of customer resentment. DVDs had just arrived: light, cheap to post, durable. Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph saw an opportunity to rent by mail.

Netflix's early years were rocky: pay-per-rental didn't work well. The breakthrough was a **monthly subscription** with no due dates or late fees, plus a queue and a recommendation engine that steered people to less popular titles (which were cheaper to stock). It was a classic Christensen low-end and new-market entrant: worse on immediacy, better on convenience, selection and price for a segment Blockbuster ignored.
Netflix has made at least four company-defining bets:
points: **DVD subscription (1999)**: recurring revenue and no late fees.
**Streaming (2007)**: cannibalise its own DVD business as broadband spread. The 2011 **Qwikster** split and price change angered customers; Netflix reversed the split but kept pushing streaming.
**Originals (2013 onwards)**: *House of Cards*, *Orange Is the New Black*, then films, local-language series and animation, using data on what members watch to inform bets.
**Global launch (2016)**: expand to about 130 countries simultaneously, then invest in local content — Korean, Spanish, Indian.

**Ads and password sharing (2022–23)**: after losing subscribers in early 2022 for the first time in about a decade, Netflix launched a cheaper ad-supported plan and cracked down on account sharing, after years of resisting both.

notes.p:
Blockbuster went bankrupt in 2010. Netflix became the world's largest subscription streaming service, with well over 200 million paid memberships by the early 2020s, and it began winning major awards for its originals. When Disney, Warner and others launched competing services and pulled content, Netflix's head start in originals, global reach and recommendation technology held up. After the 2022 setback, the ad tier and password-sharing crackdown restored subscriber growth and profitability; in 2025 Netflix stopped reporting quarterly subscriber numbers, emphasising revenue and engagement instead.

In India, Netflix found the market tough: low prices, strong local players (JioCinema/JioHotstar, Prime Video) and mobile-first viewing. It responded with a mobile-only plan and price cuts in 2021 while investing in Indian originals.
Illustrative India numbers for a mobile plan.
points: Monthly price ₹149; contribution after payment fees and streaming costs, say 40% → **₹59.6 per month**.
Monthly churn 5% → average lifetime = 1 ÷ 0.05 = **20 months**.
If acquiring a subscriber costs ₹600 in marketing and free trials, LTV/CAC ≈ 1,192 ÷ 600 ≈ **2.0** — acceptable but not great (many investors like 3×).
Cutting churn to 4% raises lifetime to 25 months and LTV to ₹1,490 — a 25% gain without raising price. That is why content cadence and recommendations (which reduce churn) matter so much.
