Content fixed-cost logic: a ₹200 crore Indian series spread over 1 crore Indian subscribers is ₹200 each; over 5 crore, just ₹40.

notes.p: Netflix argued that in creative work, the best people are many times more valuable than average ones, so it should hire top talent, pay top of market, remove controls (no fixed vacation policy, simple expense policy: 'act in Netflix's best interests'), and share context rather than control. The **keeper test** and generous severance for adequate performers keep 'talent density' high. Critics say the culture can feel harsh and insecure, and that it fits a high-margin creative company more than, say, a factory or a bank.

points: **Disrupt yourself** before others do: DVD → streaming.
**Customer anger is costly** (Qwikster) — communicate changes and pace them.
**Supplier power can force vertical integration**: licensing → originals.
**Scale economics** in content: fixed costs spread over a global base create a flywheel.
**Strategic flexibility**: ads and password crackdowns were reversals of earlier positions when conditions changed.
**Culture is a system** tied to the business model; copy it carefully.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** You run Netflix India. A rival bundles cricket, films and series cheaply with a giant telecom base. Do you (a) cut prices further and push the ad tier, (b) bid for live sports, (c) partner with telecom operators for bundled plans, or (d) stay premium and invest in fewer, bigger Indian originals? Use LTV, churn and content-cost-per-subscriber logic to defend your choice.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Product and marketing interviews love subscription metrics: churn, LTV, CAC, ARPU and engagement — be ready to compute LTV from price, margin and churn. Strategy courses use Netflix for self-disruption, vertical integration and global expansion; OB courses debate its culture deck. Media, consumer-tech and strategy roles all expect you to reason about content as a fixed cost spread across a subscriber base.

points: Founded 1997 (Hastings, Randolph); DVD-by-mail → subscription (1999), no late fees.
Blockbuster reportedly declined to buy Netflix (~$50m, 2000); bankrupt 2010.
Streaming 2007; **Qwikster** misstep 2011.
Originals from *House of Cards* (2013): answer to studios' supplier power.
Global launch 2016 (~130 countries); India mobile plan 2019, price cuts 2021.
Ad tier and password-sharing crackdown after 2022 subscriber loss.
Culture: freedom & responsibility, keeper test (*No Rules Rules*, 2020).
LTV = monthly contribution ÷ churn; content is a fixed cost per subscriber.

chapters.title: Case: Nokia and Kodak — why great incumbents fail

cards.title: Two giants, one pattern
cards.body: **Kodak** dominated photography for a century; **Nokia** was the world's largest mobile phone maker from the late 1990s into the early 2010s. Both saw the new technology coming — Kodak even **invented** an early digital camera — yet both lost their core businesses. Why do smart, well-funded leaders fail?

cards.title: Kodak's razor-and-blade model
cards.body: George Eastman's Kodak sold cameras cheaply and made its money on **film, paper, chemicals and processing** — recurring, high-margin sales every time you took a photo. 'You press the button, we do the rest.' Digital photography needed no film. Every digital success cannibalised the profit engine.

cards.title: Kodak saw it coming
cards.body: In 1975 Kodak engineer **Steve Sasson** built one of the first digital cameras. Kodak invested in digital and even led US digital camera sales for a period in the mid-2000s — but cameras earned thin margins, and then **smartphones** killed most standalone cameras. Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection in **2012**.

cards.title: Fujifilm: the counter-example
cards.body: Japan's Fujifilm faced the same collapse of film. It **cut costs hard** and redeployed its chemistry and imaging know-how into **healthcare, materials and even cosmetics** (film and skin both rely on collagen and anti-oxidation chemistry). A textbook use of **core competence** to escape a dying market.

cards.title: Nokia's fall
cards.body: Nokia led on rugged, cheap, well-distributed phones — the Nokia 1100 was an iconic phone in India. After the **iPhone (2007)** and **Android (2008)**, the battle shifted to software and app ecosystems. Nokia's Symbian platform was hard to modernise, and internal politics slowed decisions.

cards.title: The burning platform
cards.body: In 2011 new CEO **Stephen Elop** wrote a 'burning platform' memo and bet on Microsoft's **Windows Phone** instead of Android. It didn't catch up. In 2013 Nokia agreed to sell its phone business to Microsoft. Nokia survived by refocusing on **network equipment**, buying Alcatel-Lucent (2016).

cards.title: The common causes
cards.body: (1) **Profit-model trap**: the new thing earns less than the old. (2) **Ecosystem shift**: value moves from hardware to software/platforms. (3) **Organisational fear and politics**: bad news doesn't travel up. (4) **Identity**: 'we are a film company'. Grove's strategic inflection points and Christensen's dilemma, in real life.

cards.q: Which company invented an early digital camera but later went bankrupt?
cards.explain: Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built an early digital camera in 1975; Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

cards.q: Fujifilm survived the decline of film mainly by:
options: Redeploying its chemistry and imaging competencies into new industries
cards.explain: It applied core competencies to healthcare, materials and cosmetics while cutting film costs.

cards.q: The deepest cause of Nokia's smartphone decline was:
options: Failure to adapt as value shifted to software platforms and app ecosystems
cards.explain: The competition moved from devices to ecosystems (iOS, Android), where Nokia lagged.

notes.p:
**Kodak**, founded by George Eastman in the 1880s, made photography a mass habit with cheap cameras and the slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest'. For most of the 20th century it dominated film in the US and was a global household name. Its profit came from **consumables** — film, paper, chemicals and photo finishing.

**Nokia**, a Finnish company that began in 1865 as a paper mill and later made rubber boots and cables, refocused on mobile phones in the 1990s under Jorma Ollila. It became the world's largest phone maker around 1998, with superb supply chains, durable hardware and a massive emerging-market presence. In India, Nokia was close to synonymous with 'mobile phone' in the 2000s and ran a large factory near Chennai.

points: **Kodak** invested in digital research and products, but strategy was shaped by the need to protect film margins. It pursued digital cameras, online photo services and printing, and a push into consumer and commercial inkjet printing — mostly lower-margin businesses.
**Nokia** stuck with its Symbian operating system and hardware-led culture after the iPhone; it ran several overlapping software efforts (Symbian versions, MeeGo) that competed internally.

**Nokia, 2011**: Stephen Elop's 'burning platform' memo admitted Nokia was losing; he chose to partner with Microsoft on Windows Phone rather than adopt Android, to avoid becoming a commodity Android maker.
**Fujifilm** (counter-case) cut its film workforce and capacity sharply, then bought and built businesses in medical imaging, pharmaceuticals, display materials and cosmetics.

notes.p:
Film sales collapsed through the 2000s as digital and then smartphone photography took over. Kodak's digital-camera business briefly did well but at thin margins, and then phone cameras shrank the whole camera market. Kodak filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in January 2012 and emerged in 2013 as a much smaller company focused on commercial printing and imaging.

Nokia's phone market share fell rapidly from 2010 onward; Windows Phone never gained enough apps or users. In 2013 Nokia agreed to sell its devices business to Microsoft (completed in 2014), which later wrote much of it off. Nokia reinvented itself as a telecom-network equipment company and bought Alcatel-Lucent in 2016. In India, Nokia was also slow to respond to cheap **dual-SIM** phones from local brands, a small but telling miss.

Research by Quy Huy and Timo Vuori (published around 2015) based on interviews with Nokia managers argued that a climate of **fear** — top managers afraid of losing investors and middle managers afraid of telling bosses bad news — slowed Nokia's response.
Illustrative numbers for one Kodak household customer in the film era vs the digital era.
points: **Film**: a family shoots 4 rolls a year. Film plus processing and prints bring Kodak about **$40 a year** at a 60% margin → **$24 profit a year**, every year.
**Digital**: the same family buys a $200 digital camera every 4 years at a 15% margin → $30 profit per 4 years = **$7.50 a year**, and most photos are never printed.
Profit per customer falls from $24 to $7.50 — about **69% lower** ((24 − 7.5) ÷ 24 ≈ 0.69).

Even if Kodak won the digital camera market, its profit pool would shrink by two-thirds. Then smartphones removed even the camera sale. That is why 'just go digital' was never a full answer — Kodak needed a new profit model, as Fujifilm found.
**Seeing is not enough**: both firms saw the technology; the problem was their **profit model, organisation and identity**.
**Value migrates**: from consumables to devices (Kodak), from devices to platforms (Nokia). Ask where profit will sit in five years.
**Core competence offers escape routes**: Fujifilm redeployed what it was good at; Kodak defined itself by a product.
**Psychological safety matters**: fear blocks bad news (Senge, Deming's 'drive out fear').
**Bet decisively at inflection points** (Grove) — Nokia's multiple overlapping platforms wasted precious years.
**Survival can look different**: Nokia lives on as a network company — reinvention is possible.

notes.p: **Discussion question:** It is 2008. You are Nokia's CEO. You still sell more phones than anyone, mostly cheap and mid-range devices, and you are very profitable. The iPhone has just reset expectations, and Google is giving Android away free to phone makers. Do you (a) adopt Android and compete on hardware and distribution, (b) rebuild your own modern operating system from scratch, (c) partner with Microsoft, or (d) double down on cheap phones for emerging markets? What does each choice do to your margins, your developers, your identity and your speed?

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews, exams and jobs
notes.p: Strategy exams use Kodak and Nokia to illustrate the innovator's dilemma, strategic inflection points and value migration; mention Fujifilm for a balanced answer. Interviewers ask 'Which company do you think is the next Kodak?' — pick an incumbent whose profit model is threatened (e.g. a business that bills by effort in the age of AI) and explain the mechanism, not just the technology.

points: Kodak: razor-and-blade (cheap cameras, profitable film); Sasson's digital camera (1975); bankruptcy 2012.
Profit-model trap: digital earned far less per customer than film.
**Fujifilm** escaped by redeploying competencies (healthcare, materials, cosmetics).
Nokia: world's largest phone maker ~1998 onward; iPhone 2007 + Android 2008 shifted value to ecosystems.
Elop's 'burning platform' (2011); Windows Phone; devices sold to Microsoft (2013–14); Alcatel-Lucent (2016).
Fear and politics slowed Nokia (Huy & Vuori).
Frameworks: Christensen, Grove, Prahalad, Senge.

chapters.title: MBA career paths: what each job actually is

cards.title: Why choose deliberately
cards.body: An MBA opens many doors, but each job is a very different daily life. Choosing well means understanding the **actual work**, the hours, the skills rewarded and where it leads in 5–10 years — not just the starting salary or the brand on the offer letter.

cards.title: Management consulting
cards.body: Firms like McKinsey, BCG and Bain, plus Big Four advisory and Accenture Strategy. You solve a client's business problem in 6–12 week projects: interviews, data analysis, Excel models, slides, and workshops with senior executives. **Skills**: structured thinking, communication, speed. **Life**: travel, long hours, rapid learning. **Exits**: strategy roles, startups, PE.

cards.title: Investment banking
cards.body: Advising companies on **M&A**, raising equity (IPOs) and debt. Associates build **financial models** and valuation, write pitch books and manage deal processes. Indian players include Kotak, Avendus, JM Financial and Axis Capital; global banks include Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley. **Life**: very long hours, deal-driven. **Exits**: PE, corporate development, CFO track.

cards.title: Product management
cards.body: A **PM** decides *what* to build and *why*: understanding users, prioritising features, writing specs, working daily with engineers and designers, and owning metrics like retention or conversion. Employers: Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, PhonePe, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, SaaS firms. **Skills**: user empathy, data, tech fluency, influence without authority.

cards.title: Marketing / brand management
cards.body: At FMCG firms (HUL, P&G, ITC, Nestlé, Marico), an MBA often starts with a **sales stint** in the field, then becomes an assistant brand manager — the 'mini-CEO' of a brand: consumer insight, positioning, pricing, packs, ad campaigns with agencies, and P&L tracking. **Skills**: consumer understanding, analytics, cross-functional coordination.

cards.title: Operations, GM and entrepreneurship
cards.body: **Operations/supply chain**: plants, logistics, procurement, e-commerce fulfilment (Amazon, Tata Steel, Asian Paints). **General management programmes**: rotations across functions, e.g. Tata Administrative Services or Aditya Birla Group's leadership programmes. **Entrepreneurship**: B-school incubators like IIM Ahmedabad's CIIE help students start up; some schools offer placement deferral.

cards.title: Comparing two offers
cards.body: Offer A: CTC ₹32 lakh = ₹24 fixed + ₹4 variable + ₹4 one-time joining bonus. Offer B: CTC ₹28 lakh = ₹25 fixed + ₹3 variable. If A's variable pays out at 75% and B's at 90%, **recurring** pay: A = 24 + 3 = ₹27 lakh; B = 25 + 2.7 = ₹27.7 lakh. B is better from year 2 despite the lower headline CTC.

cards.q: Which role primarily involves building financial models, valuation and pitch books for M&A and IPOs?
cards.explain: Investment bankers advise on deals; associates model, value and prepare pitch materials.

cards.q: A product manager's core responsibility is:
options: Deciding what to build and why, and owning outcome metrics
cards.explain: PMs define the problem, prioritise, and own metrics; engineers build.

cards.q: Offer X: ₹20 lakh fixed + ₹5 lakh variable (expected payout 60%). Offer Y: ₹22 lakh fixed + ₹2 lakh variable (expected payout 100%). Expected recurring pay?

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
A two-year MBA is, among other things, a **career switch machine**. Most students come in to change function (engineer → product or consulting), industry (IT → FMCG), or level (individual contributor → manager). Each career path rewards different strengths and has its own culture, hours and long-term trajectory. The worst mistake is picking a job for its headline CTC or prestige, then discovering you dislike the daily work.

A useful test for each path: **What do I actually do on a Tuesday afternoon? What does a great performer look like? Where are people from this job in ten years?**

points: **Consulting**: strategy (MBB), operations, technology and Big Four advisory. A typical project: 'Should our client enter the EV-charging market?' — you build a market model, interview experts, run customer surveys and present a recommendation. Steep learning; frequent travel; you move between industries every few months.

**Investment banking & finance**: M&A, equity and debt capital markets; plus private equity/venture capital (usually after some years), corporate finance, treasury and fintech. Precision and stamina matter; one wrong cell in a model can cost credibility.

**Product management**: discovery (what problem?), prioritisation (what first?), delivery (with engineering) and measurement (did it work?). Tech-background MBAs often choose PM; non-tech MBAs can too with demonstrated user and data skills.
**Marketing**: brand management in FMCG, consumer durables, auto and digital firms; also category and growth marketing in tech. Expect a sales/rural stint early in FMCG.
**Operations & supply chain**: manufacturing, procurement, logistics, quality, and e-commerce operations; heavy on Excel, lean thinking and people management on the ground.
**General management / leadership programmes**: rotational roles leading to business-unit leadership.
**Entrepreneurship**: incubators, alumni networks and seed funding; some top schools let students defer placements and return later.

notes.h: Real examples: what the first year looks like
notes.p: A **consulting** associate at a strategy firm in Mumbai may spend three months on a cost-reduction project for a cement company, then two months on a market-entry study for a global consumer brand. A **brand management** trainee at an FMCG major may spend months in a rural sales territory in Uttar Pradesh, learning distributor economics, before joining the brand team for a shampoo. A **PM** at a fintech firm may own the UPI payment-success rate and spend the year running experiments to lift it by a few percentage points — which can mean crores in transactions. An **IB** associate in Mumbai may work on a mid-cap company's IPO: due diligence, the prospectus, valuation and investor presentations.

notes.h: Worked example: reading an offer properly
notes.p: CTC ('cost to company') in India bundles many components. Learn to separate them.
points: **Fixed pay**: guaranteed salary.
**Variable / performance bonus**: paid only if targets are met; ask for typical payout history.
**Joining / sign-on bonus**: one-time; may have a clawback if you leave within a year.
**Retention bonus, ESOPs/RSUs**: vest over years; value depends on the company's share price.
**Benefits**: PF contributions, insurance, housing — sometimes included in CTC.

Example: Offer A ₹32 lakh (₹24 fixed + ₹4 variable at 75% expected payout + ₹4 joining) vs Offer B ₹28 lakh (₹25 fixed + ₹3 variable at 90%). Year-1 expected: A = 24 + 3 + 4 = **₹31 lakh**; B = 25 + 2.7 = **₹27.7 lakh**. Year-2 onward: A = **₹27 lakh**; B = **₹27.7 lakh**. Headline CTC overstated A's lasting advantage.

notes.h: Choosing your path: a simple framework
notes.p: Score each path from 1–5 on four questions, weighting by what matters to you:
points: **Energy**: do the tasks energise you (analysis, people, creativity, building)?
**Edge**: do your past experience and skills give you a head start?
**Exit options**: where does this path lead in 5–10 years?
**Economics & lifestyle**: pay, hours, travel, location, stability.
Talk to at least three people in each role — alumni are the best source — before deciding.

notes.p: Chasing 'Day 0' brand names without wanting the job; applying to every function and preparing for none deeply; ignoring the first 2–3 years' learning curve in favour of a slightly higher CTC; assuming consulting or IB are the only 'successful' outcomes; and underestimating how much the **first manager and team** shape your growth.

notes.h: How it shows up in interviews and jobs
notes.p: Every placement interview opens with some version of 'Why this role?' A convincing answer links your past, the role's actual work, and your future goal. Consulting firms test with **case interviews**; banks with **technical finance** questions (valuation, accounting); PM interviews with **product design and metrics** questions; FMCG with **marketing cases** and consumer insight questions.

points: Choose by **daily work**, skills rewarded and 5–10 year exits — not just CTC.
**Consulting**: client problems, models, slides; MBB, Big Four, Accenture.
**IB**: M&A, IPOs, debt; modelling and pitch books; long hours.
**PM**: what to build and why; owns metrics.
**Marketing**: brand 'mini-CEO'; FMCG starts with sales stints.
**Ops, GM programmes, entrepreneurship** (incubators like CIIE; placement deferral).
Read offers: fixed vs variable vs one-time; compare **recurring** pay.

chapters.title: Internships, PPOs and placements: building your story and CV

cards.title: The Indian B-school calendar
cards.body: In a typical 2-year programme, **summer placements** (for an 8–10 week internship) happen in the **first few months of year 1**. The internship runs between year 1 and year 2 (roughly April–June). **Final placements** happen in the second half of year 2. So you must have a career story ready within weeks of joining.

cards.title: Internships and PPOs
cards.body: A strong internship can earn a **PPO** (pre-placement offer) — a full-time job offer before final placements. Some firms offer a **PPI** (pre-placement interview) instead. PPOs reduce pressure in year 2; many top firms fill a big share of their full-time roles this way. Treat the internship as a 10-week job interview.

cards.title: How placement days work
cards.body: Many schools group recruiters into **days, clusters or cohorts** by profile, so firms of similar standing come together. Rules often limit how many offers you can hold, and accepting an offer typically takes you out of the process. Leading schools publish **audited placement reports** under standards like IPRS.

cards.title: The one-page CV
cards.body: Top Indian B-schools use a strict **one-page** format. Each bullet should follow **action + task + quantified result**: 'Automated vendor reconciliation, cutting monthly closing time from 10 to 6 days (−40%) for a ₹300 crore portfolio.' Numbers, ownership and scale beat adjectives.

cards.title: Your story: past → MBA → future
cards.body: Interviewers want a **coherent narrative**: what you did before, why the MBA, and why *this* role is the logical next step. 'I spent three years building payment features as an engineer, saw that the hardest questions were which features to build, and want to move into product management.' Every CV bullet should support the story.

cards.title: Preparation by role
cards.body: **Consulting**: practise 30–50 case interviews and guesstimates with peers. **Finance**: accounting, valuation (DCF, multiples), markets news. **PM**: product design, metrics, prioritisation. **Marketing**: brand cases, consumer insight. Corporate **case competitions** such as HUL LIME, Mahindra War Room and Tata Crucible can add visible achievements.

cards.title: Fixing a weak CV bullet
cards.body: Weak: 'Responsible for handling client escalations.' Strong: 'Led a 4-member team resolving client escalations; reduced average resolution time from 72 to 30 hours (−58%) and lifted CSAT from 3.6 to 4.3.' Check the maths: (72 − 30) ÷ 72 = 0.583 → 58%.

cards.q: A PPO is:
options: A pre-placement offer of a full-time job, usually after a summer internship
cards.explain: PPO = pre-placement offer, typically earned through internship performance.

cards.q: Processing time fell from 50 days to 35 days. The percentage reduction is:
Which CV bullet is strongest?
options: Built a churn model that identified 12% of at-risk users, reducing monthly churn from 5% to 4.2%
Hard-working team player with great communication skills
cards.explain: It shows action, scale and a quantified result.

notes.h: The core idea in plain words
notes.p:
In Indian B-schools, career outcomes are shaped very early. Summer internship recruitment usually starts within the first few months of the programme — often before you've finished your first term. A great internship can turn into a pre-placement offer, which can decide your first post-MBA job a year before graduation. So the career work starts on day one: **pick a direction, build a story, prepare a sharp CV, and practise interviews** for that direction.

The process is competitive but very structured. Understanding the rules lets you spend effort where it matters.

points: **Months 1–2**: career exploration — alumni talks, company presentations, club sessions (consulting, finance, marketing, product clubs). Shortlist 1–2 target functions.
**CV preparation**: one-page format, reviewed by seniors and the placement committee; points must be verifiable.
**Summer placements**: firms shortlist based on CVs; group discussions, case interviews, technical and HR rounds, often compressed into a few intense days.
**Internship (8–10 weeks)**: a live project with a final presentation to senior managers.
**PPO/PPI**: offered based on performance and fit.
**Final placements**: for students without PPOs, or those who want to try other firms; organised in days/clusters/cohorts by many schools.
**Lateral placements**: for students with significant prior experience, sometimes run separately.
Offer rules: limits on holding offers, and accepting one usually exits you from the process.

notes.p:
Your story connects three points: **past**, **MBA**, **future**. It must be honest and consistent across CV, essays and interviews.

A good formula: **'I did X, where I learnt Y and discovered I enjoy Z. The MBA gives me A and B. That's why this role, at this firm, is the right next step.'** Example: an engineer from a steel plant targeting operations consulting: 'Three years in a steel plant showed me how small process changes — like cutting furnace downtime — created crores in savings. I want to solve such problems across many companies, which is why operations consulting fits.'

Avoid: a different story for each company, vague passion statements ('I love strategy'), and claims you can't support with evidence.

notes.h: Worked example: writing quantified CV bullets
notes.p: Use **action verb + what you did + result with numbers + scale**. Always check your arithmetic — interviewers do.
points: Raw: 'Improved warehouse efficiency.'
Facts: picking time per order fell from 12 minutes to 9; 4,000 orders a day.
Time saved per day: 3 min × 4,000 = 12,000 min = **200 hours a day**.
Final bullet: 'Redesigned pick paths in a 4,000-order/day warehouse, cutting picking time per order by 25% (12 → 9 min), saving ~200 labour-hours daily.'
If your impact is hard to quantify, use scale (team size, budget, number of users) or recognition (top 5% performer, award).

notes.p: **Consulting** firms run case interviews: a business problem ('profits of a cement company fell 20% — why?') solved aloud with structure, numbers and a recommendation; plus guesstimates ('How many ATMs are there in India?'). **Banks** ask accounting and valuation (walk through a DCF; how does ₹10 of depreciation flow through the statements?). **PM** interviews test product sense ('improve WhatsApp for small businesses'), metrics and prioritisation. **FMCG** firms test marketing judgement and grit (rural sales readiness). Everyone asks 'Tell me about yourself', 'Why this role?', a failure story and a leadership story — prepare these using the **STAR** method (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

Clarify the problem statement and success metric in week one; meet your mentor weekly; talk to people across functions; give a mid-term update; and end with a crisp, data-backed recommendation the business can act on. Show ownership — PPO decisions weigh **attitude and fit** as much as analysis. Ask for feedback early, not at the final presentation.

Applying to everything with a generic CV; inflating claims you can't defend; preparing cases only in the last week; neglecting peer practice groups; treating the internship as a holiday; and panicking if you don't get a PPO — many students land excellent roles in final placements or laterally later.

points: Summers recruitment comes early in year 1; internship of ~8–10 weeks between years.
**PPO** = pre-placement offer; **PPI** = pre-placement interview.
Finals: days/clusters/cohorts; offer-holding rules; audited reports (IPRS).
**One-page CV**: action + task + quantified result; verify maths.
**Story**: past → MBA → future, consistent everywhere.
Prepare by role: cases (consulting), valuation (finance), product sense (PM), marketing cases (FMCG).
Use **STAR** for behavioural answers; treat the internship as a 10-week interview.
